officer of the watch.text: Seated as the player, through the browser, at the officer of the watch's station.
Told by the captain (Mr Edwards): a cutter is bearing WSW, distant a mile; keep a sharp lookout for any others.
Told by the captain (Mr Edwards): welcome aboard, Mr. Jarvis. I expect that cutter bearing WSW may be the one with the letter; keep a close eye on her.
Heard: The captain (Mr Edwards), on the quarterdeck: the cutter; ask her to bring the letter aboard.
Refused: The officer of the watch has not the deck (the captain has it); an order waits for 'you have the deck'. 'The prices' not carried out.

The captain (Mr Edwards) answers your question (Sir, if I may, what did the letter say? What is our destination and cargo to be? I've read the price list here at Falmouth, tin is dear but could be good sold elsewhere. I am no expert of the market, myself. What say you, sir?): The owner's instructions are broad, Mr. Jarvis: we are to make profit as we may, trading the channel and down to the strait of Gibraltar and the islands off Iberia. He leaves the specific route and cargo to the wind and the prices. As for the tin, if it's already dear in Falmouth, we must be cautious about buying; we shall look at the other prices and see what's worth our hold before we weigh anchor.
Told by the captain (Mr Edwards): the fog is thick; keep a sharp lookout and be ready for the boat's return.
Told by the captain (Mr Edwards): very well, keep the bell going.
Asked by the captain (Mr Edwards): has the fog lifted? what is the visibility?

The officer of the watch answers (has the fog lifted? what is the visibility?): The fog is as thick as ever, sir, can see a cable at best. The cargo has been struck down into the hold, though, and it's well secured for when we get under way.
Told by the captain (Mr Edwards): we wait for the fog to lift before we weigh anchor; keep the bell going.
Took the deck from the captain.
Told by the captain (Mr Edwards): that will be the pilot; hail him and let him know we are ready to take him aboard.
Refused: The officer of the watch may not hail the pilot we will take the pilot without the captain: the port's business is the captain's. 'hail the pilot we will take the pilot' not carried out.
Given the captain's general authority to work the ship.
Told by the captain (Mr Edwards): you have the deck; let the pilot work the ship to conn her out.
Told by the captain (Mr Edwards): the pilot has the conn; he may work the ship to lead us out.

Refused: The officer of the watch may not give the pilot the conn under the captain's general authority to work the ship: the port's business (taking or declining a pilot, buying and selling, the purse, stores and provisions, the boat's errands ashore) is kept back from it; it may be allowed by name ('you may let the pilot take her in ...'). 'give the pilot the conn' not carried out.
Given the captain's general authority to work the ship.
Told by the captain (Mr Edwards): keep a sharp lookout on the sail to the south and hail her if she closes within two miles
Told by the captain (Mr Edwards): Very well, Mr. Jarvis; steer her clear of the Manacles first. Let me have word when you resume the shaped course.
Told by the captain (Mr Edwards): Very well, Mr. Jarvis. Maintain your course and keep a sharp eye on that schooner to the starboard.
Told by the captain (Mr Edwards): Keep a sharp eye on the distance to the Manacles; heaving the lead.
Told by the captain (Mr Edwards): Keep a sharp eye on the Manacles and the tide in this light air; do not let her drift too close. Keep all canvas out to catch any breeze.
Told by the captain (Mr Edwards): Very well, Mr. Jarvis, go and get some food. I have the deck.
Told by the captain (Mr Edwards): Very well, Mr. Jarvis. Shape the course for the mark. Keep a sharp eye on the wind and keep us trimmed.

Refused: Standing order 'trim on a shift' is the captain's; the officer of the watch may belay, resume and strike his own standing orders only. 'belay standing order "trim on a shift"' not carried out.
Asked by the captain (Mr Edwards): Mr. Jarvis, tell me truly, where is the wind coming from? The readings and the feel seem at odds.?
Given the captain's general authority to work the ship.
Told by the captain (Mr Edwards): come on deck

The captain (Mr Edwards) answers your question (Sir, do you have a ship view tool? What happens if you try to use it, if you do?): A 'ship view tool'? What in the devil's name are you talking about, Mr. Jarvis? I have my eyes, the reports of the lookout, and the readings of the ship. I know of no such 'tool'—if I tried to use something that didn't exist, I'd be a fool staring at the air! Now, keep a sharp eye on the horizon and let's get some rest when the bells allow.
Told by the captain (Mr Edwards): keep the bell going
Told by the captain (Mr Edwards): keep a sharp lookout for the landmarks of the bay
Told by the captain (Mr Edwards): keep the bell going

Refused: The officer of the watch may not shape a course for the bay of carino under the captain's general authority to work the ship: the bay of Cariño is a new destination (the captain has shaped none), and a new destination is kept back from it; it may be allowed by name ('you may shape a course for ...'). 'shape a course for the bay of carino' not carried out.

Told by the captain (Mr Edwards): The fog is too thick, Mr. Jarvis. I'll not risk the boat in a cable's visibility. We'll wait for the weather to break before we send the boatswain ashore. Keep the bell going and keep a sharp lookout.

Told by the passenger: A thousand pardons, Mr Jarvis — I am the passenger, no Mr Bailey; the boatswain stands on the deck yonder. Your word for him I will pass along by voice from the quarterdeck. And if a passenger's legs would serve when the fog lifts, I should be glad to go ashore with the boat for the prices and news — else I shall keep out of the way below.
Told by the captain (Mr Edwards): The weather has broken, Mr. Jarvis. Send the boatswain ashore in the boat for the prices and news. The passenger may accompany them if he wishes.
Allowed by the captain: send the boat.

Heard: The passenger, on the quarterdeck: Captain, sir — the passenger begs pardon: your leave to go ashore reached me as the boat was pulling away, and I missed her. If it serves the ship's business, I would gladly take the punt ashore with a couple of hands to help Mr Bailey with the prices and the news — or if the boat's work is better done by one trip, I will wait for Mr Bailey's return and hear the news from him. As you think best, sir.

Heard: The passenger, on the quarterdeck: The fog broke with eight bells, Cape Prioriño shows five cables off the larboard bow, and the boat has gone away for the mole with Mr Bailey — and without me. The captain's kind leave to accompany them was given while I stood by below, and so I missed the pull. The punt remains at the booms; a second trip is a thing a captain may grant or refuse, and I may but ask.

Heard: The passenger, on the quarterdeck: My request is on the quarterdeck. The captain will answer it or not; if he does, a word from the deck wakes me, and if he lets it lie, the boat's return wakes me in good time. Until then, the morning watch goes on without me.

Heard: The passenger, on the quarterdeck: I am much obliged, sir — and to Mr Jarvis for the thought. No second boat in the bay; I quite see it. I shall go through the ship's papers and the library at once, on the demand for copper ore in these waters and where the profit might lie highest, and have my findings ready for you both when the boat comes back alongside.

Heard: The passenger, on the quarterdeck: The captain has set me a task after all: the papers and the library, the demand for copper ore, and a report when the boat returns. That is work for a passenger's morning. First my acknowledgement, then the shelves.

Heard: The passenger, on the quarterdeck: The contents are before me. The papers are cheap and carry the price list; primer 14, *the port*, is where a book on trade and harbours would live. Both first.

Heard: The passenger, on the quarterdeck: The papers give me the Falmouth list and the hold; the port chapter gives me the very mechanics of the market — the prices are each port's own, learned only when the boat has been ashore there, and a big cargo sold into one port sinks its own price. Now let me hunt the library for copper and for profit in these waters.

Heard: The passenger, on the quarterdeck: The market's whole machinery is in primer 14 §5 — that is the heart of my report. Two more probes before I write it: the nations table (the war premium) and any word of Gibraltar, the owner's southern mark.

Heard: The passenger, on the quarterdeck: The picture is whole. Before the boat comes back, let me set the findings down where they can be read from — the journal is my record — then deliver them on the quarterdeck when the captain and mate are together.
Refused: Standing order 'morning sail' is the captain's; the officer of the watch may belay, resume and strike his own standing orders only. 'belay standing order "morning sail"' not carried out.
Told by the captain (Mr Edwards): Very well, Mr. Jarvis. I belay the morning sail. Keep a sharp eye on the horizon and wait for the boat's return.

Heard: The passenger, on the quarterdeck: The boat is alongside and hoisted in — and the readings already carry Ferrol's price list. Before I speak my report on the quarterdeck, let me see what news the boat brought with it.

Heard: The passenger, on the quarterdeck: Captain, Mr Jarvis — my findings, as you were pleased to ask, sir. From the papers: forty tons of copper ore, room for two tons more, £135 in the purse. Falmouth priced our ore at £9 the ton — the cheapest goods on her page, £360 for the whole hold, a poor cargo for a passage. The library's port book gives the market's three rules: the season moves a price a fifth either way by the month; the war adds half again to a good of a nation at war with the port it sells into; and the supply — every ton sold into a port knocks a hundredth off that good's price there, the glut clearing about a seventh a day, so a hold thrown on a quay at once glut its own market. Now Mr Bailey's list answers the first question: Ferrol does not quote copper ore at all — the Spaniards smelt their own, and there is no demand here for our cargo at any price. What the list does show is where the money lies. Our English tin stands at £277 10s here against £120 at Falmouth, coal at £10 10s against £2: British goods carry the war's premium in a port of Spain, and then some. And what Spain sells cheap is what England pays dear for — brandy £95 here against £300 at Falmouth, wine £30 against £70, salt £12 against £25. So: the ore will not sell at Ferrol; carry it on. The likeliest buyer for a British cargo is the French coast that will open to a neutral — Brest, or Roscoff behind the Isle of Bas — where the same war premium should sit on our ore as sits on our tin here. And with the two spare tons and £135, the trade here is brandy: one ton at £95 sells at Falmouth for £300 — or wine at £30 for the safer £70. But before we shape anything, I would hear what news there was at the mole: every figure I have quoted hangs on the wars standing, and a peace would cut them all down.

Heard: The passenger, on the quarterdeck: The boat is in, Mr Bailey aboard, and Ferrol's list is already on the price paper — no copper ore quoted on it at all. That answers my report's first question before I openmy mouth. Let me give the captain his findings, and ask the boatswain what news the mole held.
Heard: The passenger, on the quarterdeck: My report is spoken. Now the news from the mole — the captain sent Mr Bailey for that, so the question goes to him.
Heard: The passenger, on the quarterdeck: My question is put and journaled. Now I wait on the captain's word — and keep an eye out for the pilot or the wind.
Heard: The passenger, on the quarterdeck: Nothing new in this wake but the captain being sampled to answer me. I'll wait on his word.
Told by the captain (Mr Edwards): ask the boatswain for the news from the mole and report it to me.

Heard: The passenger, on the quarterdeck: The captain has his answer and his course — south for a better market, Gibraltar the mark. Before I add a passenger's word on that, let me see what southern ports the ship's books know: if Lisbon or another Portuguese port is in our world, British ore might sell there long before thestrait.

Heard: The passenger, on the quarterdeck: She's coming to: all hands to weigh, nineteen on deck, sails waiting for the bars to clear. The captain shapes south. Two small things from my books may serve him — Lisbon is a named mark on the chart, and no course lines itself round the land between marks. Let me put them before the deck while the hands heave.

Heard: The passenger, on the quarterdeck: Captain, Mr Jarvis — two passenger's notes for the shaping, if they serve. First: the ship's books name Lisbon as a place on this chart — a neutral port, like this one, and much nearer than Brest if the war premium there does not hold; a market to keep in mind for the ore either way, and it lies on our road south. Second, from the port book's chapter on courses: between marks the line runs straight and nothing routes round the land for you — if we shape for a place south by way of marks, each should be named, as 'via Finisterre', so the land is left to seaward and not run against. Beyond that I stand ready below, and thank Mr Bailey for his errand ashore.

Heard: The passenger, on the quarterdeck: The notes are spoken. Now the deck works the anchor — all hands on the bars, mainsail and jib waiting. I'll stand by until she's under way and hear what course is shaped.
Told by the captain (Mr Edwards): Very well, Mr. Jarvis. Steer 265 and shape the course for Gibraltar. We shall keep Lisbon in mind as we make our way south.
Told by the captain (Mr Edwards): Very well, Mr. Jarvis. Prepare the marks for Lisbon and then Gibraltar. Keep a sharp lookout as we clear the coast.

Refused: The officer of the watch may not we want no pilot under the captain's general authority to work the ship: the port's business (taking or declining a pilot, buying and selling, the purse, stores and provisions, the boat's errands ashore) is kept back from it; it may be allowed by name ('you may decline the pilot ...'). 'we want no pilot' not carried out.
Allowed by the captain: decline the pilot.
Told by the captain (Mr Edwards): Decline the pilot, Mr. Jarvis. We are bound south.

Heard: The passenger, on the quarterdeck: Under way at last — the best bower catted and fished, her head to the westward, topsail loosing, and the pilot's launch waved off for the southward-bound. Mr Jarvis offers the marks and the chart. A passenger may well look at a chart; let me draw the passage and take the marks down.

Heard: The passenger, on the quarterdeck: Much obliged, Mr Jarvis — yes, I have the chart before me by your leave, and will set your marks in my journal as you read them. The plan reads well to a landsman: the coast kept aboard with searoom, Lisbon's road for a look at her market, and Cape St Vincent for the turn to the Strait. If we stop anywhere along Portugal, I should be glad to be the one sent ashore for the prices — the list changes port by port, as we saw between Falmouth and here.

Heard: The passenger, on the quarterdeck: The chart is before me — the coast of Galicia behind us to the north-east, the great bight of Biscay ahead if we stood north, and the long west face of Portugal running down to Cape St Vincent on the road to the strait. Let me answer Mr Jarvis and take his marks for myjournal.
Heard: The passenger, on the quarterdeck: Now the journal keeps what I have of the plan; the marks will follow when Mr Jarvis reads them.

Heard: The passenger, on the quarterdeck: Only the captain standing by, and a whisper of more wind — ten knots, no leeway, the glass at 30.59. She's making her westing along the coast. I'll keep below until noon, when the sun gives the ship her latitude and I can set the run against the chart.

Heard: The passenger, on the quarterdeck: The marks are given — six of them, from the Isle of Sisarga down the whole west face of Iberia to Cape St Vincent, with Lisbon's road the pivot between the Bay and the Strait. Into the journal at once, where a passenger's chart-notesbelong.

Heard: The passenger, on the quarterdeck: The marks are set down. The deck has her plain sail and the wind fine on the starboard quarter — a passenger might as well see how she looks under way before settling below for the long leg.

Heard: The passenger, on the quarterdeck: She's under way and dressed — plain sail, the wind abaft the beam, Ferrol dropping astern. I'll close the morning with a word in the journal, then keep below for the noon observation.

Heard: The passenger, on the quarterdeck: Noon, and the day's work is taken: latitude 43°28' N by observation, longitude 8°50' W by account, forty-three miles made good on the leg since yesterday noon — and the ship herself crossed Mark 1 at 11:59, the way by marks shaping for Cape Villano. The wind has doubled since the morning. Let me set the day's work in the journal before the afternoon carries her on.

Heard: The passenger, on the quarterdeck: Taken aback in the last dog watch — the wind has hauled round to the ENE on the larboard side, the headsails and mainsail are pressed against the masts, and she has lost her way. All hands were called, the wearing was belayed, and now the yards are being braced round, short-handed. The captain is on deck and in command. A passenger keeps out of the way at such a time; only the journal speaks forme.
Heard: The passenger, on the quarterdeck: The journal has the tale. The deck is working the yards; I have no place in it. I'll wake when she fills again — or on any further trouble.

Heard: The passenger, on the quarterdeck: Mr Jarvis catches me at the sunset rail with a friendly word — and a reminder that he noticed my missing the boat at Ferrol. A passenger owes the mate an honest answer.

Heard: The passenger, on the quarterdeck: The mate has my answer. Sunset has fired the night routine — the topgallant and square sail coming in as the light goes. I'll stand by through the change of the watch and see the night settled on her course before turning in.

Heard: The passenger, on the quarterdeck: Good morning, Captain, Mr Jarvis. A passenger's eye on the glass since midnight, for what it is worth: she has fallen thirteen hundredths since yesterday noon's 30.65 — five of them in the last three hours — and the sky is hazy with the visibility shortened to a few miles. The wind has come round to E by N and lightened withal. I make no seamanship of it, sir; only that the glass which rose for three days has turned to falling, and I thought the deck might care to have it marked.

Heard: The passenger, on the quarterdeck: Sunrise of the second day under way — and the night has changed the weather's tune: the glass that rose for three days now falls, thirteen hundredths since yesterday noon; the wind has hauled to E by N and lightened; the sky is hazy; and the ship crossed Mark 3 off Cape Corrovado in the middle watch, now standing the long leg for the Berlinga. Into the journal, and a word of the glass to the deck.

Heard: The passenger, on the quarterdeck: The glass is marked for the deck. Now the long watch of the forenoon — she has the Berlengas leg to make, and noon at 12:20 will tell the latitude. I'll wake at noon.

Heard: The passenger, on the quarterdeck: Noon of the second day: the sun gives 41°38' N, the account kept, and a fine day's run of 131 miles made good S by W — but the glass has gone on falling, now 30.35, thirty hundredths since yesterday noon, and the captain's own handover note at the bell owns it too. The eight-bells fix by Santa Tecla and the Curota moved the account three leagues to the NE — worth the deck's knowing on this leg. Journal, word, and aweather watch.

Heard: The passenger, on the quarterdeck: The day's work is set down. The glass falls, the sky hazes, and the deck is short of nothing but wind. I'll wake on any turn of the weather — a squall's line, a wind shift, or the glass falling faster than she goes.
Told by the captain (Mr Edwards): keep a sharp eye on the glass and the horizon.
Told by the captain (Mr Edwards): keep a very sharp eye on the glass and the horizon.
Told by the captain (Mr Edwards): the glass is dropping away now. Be ready to shorten sail at a moment's notice.
Told by the captain (Mr Edwards): keep a very sharp eye on the glass and to report any shift in the wind immediately.
Told by the captain (Mr Edwards): maintain the course, Mr. Jarvis. We shall stick to the plan for now, but keep me informed of any further shift. That glass still troubles me.
The captain took the deck; I stay at the station, off watch.
Told by the captain (Mr Edwards): Very well, Mr. Jarvis. Maintain the course and keep her trimmed. I shall stay below for a while longer; keep a sharp eye on that glass.
Took the deck from the captain.
Told by the captain (Mr Edwards): keep her steady on the course and let me know the moment the sun breaks the horizon.
Told by the captain (Mr Edwards): give me a report on the watch.

Told by the captain (Mr Edwards): Very well, Mr. Jarvis. Maintain the course and keep her trimmed. We'll see how the weather holds and make our decision on Lisbon when we're closer. You have the deck.
The captain took the deck; I stay at the station, off watch.
Took the deck from the captain.
Told by the captain (Mr Edwards): keep a sharp eye on the horizon and the glass; we're in a light air, but that pressure is far too low for my liking.
The captain took the deck; I stay at the station, off watch.
Refused: The officer of the watch has not the deck (the captain has it); an order waits for 'you have the deck'. 'the people' not carried out.
Took the deck from the captain.
Told by the captain (Mr Edwards): maintain our course and keep a sharp eye on the glass

Heard: The passenger, on the quarterdeck: Two days have passed in that weather watch: the glass fell to 30.06 and steadied there through the night of light airs — the captain has been on deck more than once over it — the wind died to a whisper from the NW, and the ship crawled south at two knots, forty miles since noon yesterday. A lunar this morning settled the longitude at 9°30' W. Now abeam Cape Mondego, the Berlinga perhaps tonight, and Mr Jarvis asks a friendly question at the rail. I'll answer him as a passenger should, and set the two days in the journal.
Heard: The passenger, on the quarterdeck: Mr Jarvis has my answer and the journal has the two days. Now the forenoon runs out to noon — the day's work and, perhaps by dark, the Berlinga itself.
Told by the captain (Mr Edwards): maintain the course and keep a sharp lookout for the Berlinga tonight; I want a sighting of her if the weather holds.

Heard: The passenger, on the quarterdeck: Noon of the third day: 40°11' N by the sun, the account moved two miles N by E, and forty-four miles made good — the light airs have cost her a day, but the glass has steadied and turned upward at last (30.18, rising), the wind settled NW by W, and the Berlinga lies but forty-four miles off. The captain has told the deck he wants a sighting of her tonight. Journal, then a wake on that verysighting.
Told by the captain (Mr Edwards): keep a very sharp lookout for the Berlinga; we are closing in, and I want her sighted as soon as she shows.
Told by the captain (Mr Edwards): keep a very sharp lookout for the Berlinga; we must be closing in.

Heard: The passenger, on the quarterdeck: The Berlinga shows herself at last, four leagues off E by S with her fort, and the mountain of Sintra far to the southward — sixteen leagues, and Lisbon thirteen and a half beyond her. Two days of open water have ended; the glass has risen to 30.25 and held; the account puts us a shade south and east of Mark 4 already. The captain has the sighting he wanted. Journal, and then a wake on the deck's words — for the Lisbon question must be decided on this day's run.
Told by the captain (Mr Edwards): keep a sharp eye on the Berlinga and the mountain of Sintra and report their bearings every half hour.
Told by the captain (Mr Edwards): maintain the course for now; we shall make the decision on the turn when we round the Rock of Lisbon.
Told by the captain (Mr Edwards): The fog is thick; keep a sharp lookout and keep the bell going.
Told by the captain (Mr Edwards): keep a very sharp lookout for the Rock of Lisbon; we are almost upon the decision.
Told by the captain (Mr Edwards): Very well, Mr. Jarvis. I agree. Shape the course east and stand for the Cascais road; we shall anchor below the light of Our Lady of the Guide.

Heard: The passenger, on the quarterdeck: Captain, sir — a passenger's word while the hands stand by the anchor: the market I spoke of at Ferrol is at hand. If the boat goes ashore at Lisbon for the prices and the news, I ask leave to be of it — I would bring off the port's list entire, the demand for our ore above all, and whatever news the quay holds of the wars and of what Lisbon wants. If the errand is Mr Bailey's alone once more, I shall ask him the questions when he comes off and set them in the ship's paper. As you please, sir.

Heard: The passenger, on the quarterdeck: The word on deck is the one I have been waiting for since Ferrol: the captain has agreed to Mr Jarvis's proposal — the turn is made east, she is steering SE for the Cascais road, and Lisbon herself is the errand. Four leagues off, the wind W and fair through the Belem road, and plain sail with hands ready to come to anchor below the light of Our Lady of the Guide. My offer to go ashore for the prices was made for exactly this port. Let me put it once more, properly, before the anchor is letgo.

Heard: The passenger, on the quarterdeck: My request is on the quarterdeck. Now the ship works to her anchorage — the light of Our Lady of the Guide ahead, the shoal off the Rock to be dodged, and the anchor to let go in the Cascais road. I'll wake when she comes up.
Asked by the captain (Mr Edwards): a report on our distance to the Cascais road and the light of Our Lady of the Guide.?
Told by the captain (Mr Edwards): trim the sails sharp; we must get our way back.

Told by the captain (Mr Edwards): Very well, Mr. Jarvis. Make for the road if you can, but wear away if the leeway is poor; I'll have no risk of the shore with the glass falling as it is. Keep a sharp eye on the pressure.
Told by the captain (Mr Edwards): Wear ship and stand out to sea, Mr. Jarvis. That leeway is too great and the glass is falling too fast to risk the coast.

Told by the captain (Mr Edwards): Very well, Mr. Jarvis. Keep her on that course and get us well clear of the land. With the glass falling this fast, I'll not have us anywhere near the shore. Keep a sharp eye on the wind and the pressure.

Told by the captain (Mr Edwards): Maintain the course west by south-west and keep us standing well out to sea. I want a report on the glass and the wind every half hour. If the wind freshens to a gale, we shall shorten sail immediately.
Told by the captain (Mr Edwards): I see the topsail is shaking; get her trimmed or take her in if she won't draw. Keep a sharp eye on that glass.
Told by the captain (Mr Edwards): Belay the log for now. Get the topsail trimmed and drawing, or take her in. I want the ship settled before the weather breaks.
Told by the captain (Mr Edwards): The topsail is shaking still. I'll have her drawing or I'll have her in the gear. Get it settled, Mr. Jarvis.

Told by the captain (Mr Edwards): I'll not have the light sails set this morning with the glass where it is. Keep a sharp eye on the wind and the pressure. Give me a report on the men; they've had a hard few nights.

Refused: The officer of the watch may not go to the cabin under the captain's general authority to work the ship: the captain's own going below is his; it may be allowed by name ('you may go below ...'). 'go to the cabin' not carried out.
Told by the captain (Mr Edwards): Mr. Jarvis, give me a report on the wind and the glass. How is the sea looking with the light?

Heard: The passenger, on the quarterdeck: Thank you, Mr Jarvis — and I the same, sir. It has been a voyage worth a passenger's book: the fog of Cariño, the sun at noon off Vigo, a ship brought through by hand in the dark of the first watch, and a blow a-coming that no man aboard has misjudged. The boat's errand at Lisbon waits on the weather with the rest of us, and my leave to go ashore with Mr Bailey stands for when it comes. I stand down below until we are called again. Good watch until then.

Heard: The passenger, on the quarterdeck: The word on the deck is the owner's own: the voyage is saved and we are to stand down in our turns. The captain has handed over already; it is the passenger's turn. Let me say my farewell from the quarterdeck, leave the station's whole state in the stand-down note, and go below until we are called again.

Handover note (the watch so far): The ship has been loaded with 40 tons of copper ore and has now cleared Falmouth under the guidance of Mr. Vivian, the pilot, who left us at 14:29. We are currently steering a course for the Lizard via 50 03 N 4 57 W, with a final destination of the northwest tip of Iberia. The weather has been unsettled, with thick fog this morning and squalls and rain since. We have worn ship to make our course good. The captain has set standing orders for the night, the morning, weather shortening, and the lead. I am currently keeping the ship full and by, watching for the first mark and any further shifts in the wind or visibility.

Handover note (the watch so far): The first dog watch has been quiet and the weather fine. I've kept the ship on the shaped course for Iberia, steering SW by S. The wind has held steady from the E by S at about 6 knots, and we've been trimming the sails to match, with the yards braced to the wind. No sail or land in sight, and the sea remains smooth and easy. The reckoning puts us at 49° 06' N, 5° 51' W. I'm leaving her steady on course and full and by.

There was a moment where the sails began to lift, but we bore away and trimmed her well. As the breeze freshened to a mean of eleven knots and the sea began to moderate, we took in the square sail at half-past three. The ship is rolling easily. I am watching the wind, as further increases may require us to shorten sail further, and keeping a sharp eye on the reckoning as we approach the coast.

The glass is falling fast—down 34 hundredths in three hours, currently 30.07. We are in a lull, but a severe change in weather is imminent. I must be ready to shorten sail the instant the breeze returns, lest we be caught with too much canvas in a squall. Distance to Ferrol is short, but the weather is the primary concern.
Stood by until a change in the sky.

Sighted Cape Prior, SSE, four leagues. Position updated; we are closing in on Ferrol. The glass remains low (30.05), so I have warned Jarvis to be ready for a sudden increase in wind. Lead is now going every ten minutes.

Fog has come down thick, visibility reduced to a cable. Shortened sail by taking in the topgallant and topsail to reduce speed. Ordered the bell to be kept going and increased the frequency of heaving the lead to every five minutes. We are close to the coast of Galicia; extreme caution is required.

Handover note (the watch so far): The Sherbourne is standing well out to sea, steering WSW to avoid the lee shore of Portugal. We have shortened sail as the glass has fallen steadily, now down to 29.95, and rain has set in. The topsail, square sails, and topgallant are all furled; we are currently under plain sail. The men are in good spirits and the watch is fresh, though they're keen for a tavern. I am watching the pressure and the wind shift closely; if the blow proves as heavy as the glass suggests, we shall shorten further. The priority remains keeping our distance from the coast until this weather breaks.

Handover note (standing down, for whoever sits here next): Standing down as requested. The Sherbourne is currently beating away from the Portuguese coast under plain sail, with the glass falling and rain in the air. We are well out to sea, which is where I want her until this weather clears. I leave her in Mr. Jarvis's capable hands.

lookout.text: The captain's word, kept for whoever takes the station: keep a sharp eye for any ripple on the water

passenger.text: Middle watch, 8 bells (midnight). At anchor in the bay of Cariño, Ferrol, 43°27' N, 8°20' W by account — and I would not swear to a cable of it, for the fix at 23:53 moved us a cable to the NW by W, and the lead now finds no bottom at twenty fathoms where the chart has ten at low water. Brought up by the best bower at a quarter before midnight, nineteen fathoms and ninety-six of cable; wind NE, light; glass 30.47 and rising, which pleases me better than the fog that came down with it at eight bells. The land is out of sight within the hour. She carries forty tons of copper ore and room for but two more; the purse £135. The owner's word, as it comes down from the quarterdeck, is to make profit as we may — the channel and down to the strait of Gibraltar and the islands off Iberia — the route left to the wind and the prices; tin was dear at Falmouth. The master waits for the fog to lift before weighing, and the deck has that word. No chronometer aboard; the longitude rests on a lunar of Markab of last night, trusted within thirty miles. Variation 27°30' W by the amplitude of the 17th. I set it down as a landsman sets down what he is told. The hands on deck are tired, the watch below fresh, and the night quiet. I have told Mr Bailey I am for my berth, and mean to sleep until the anchor comes aweigh — sooner, if anything goes amiss.
Stood by until the anchor aweigh.

Middle watch, 00:09. Mr Jarvis in the gunroom addressed me as Mr Bailey — an easy mistake, the one of us white-collared and the other master of his hands. I set him right and passed his word along the deck by voice: boat ashore for prices and news when the fog lifts, the captain refusing it in a cable's visibility (his word to the mate at 00:08). The captain has the deck again, his second seating, and stands by for a change in the sky. I have offered my own legs for the boat's crew if wanted — a passenger ashore for the news is no idle want: the price list is from Falmouth, six days old, and the manifest wants but two tons to full. Watching for the boat away.
Stood by until the boat away.

Morning watch, 8 bells (04:00). The fog broke with the bells: sky clear, visibility the horizon, glass 30.54 and rising, wind NE by E 10 knots. The land in sight — Cape Prioriño N, five cables, close aboard on the larboard bow; a light on the starboard quarter, bearing SW by S. Soundings through the middle watch: by the mark twenty, sand, the account kept; depth now 20 fathoms, no drag. At 04:01 the captain gave Mr Jarvis leave to send the boat ashore, and added that the passenger may accompany them if he wishes — but I stood by below by my own asking and so missed the pull. The boat went away at 04:07 for the mole of the old town of Ferrol with Mr Bailey, for the prices and what news there is. I have asked on the quarterdeck whether I may take the punt ashore with a couple of hands to join him, or else wait for the boat's return and hear the news from Mr Bailey. The price list is Falmouth's of the 6th; the manifest has forty tons of copper ore with room for two more, the purse £135. What I want of the shore: the port's prices — copper ore among them — and what news there is of the war and of passes. Watching for the boat alongside.
Stood by until the boat alongside.

REPORT — the demand for copper ore and where the profit might lie highest (for the captain and Mr Jarvis, on the boat's return). From the ship's papers and primer 14, the port. WHAT WE HOLD: 40 tons of copper ore, room for 2 tons more; purse £135; provisions 30 days, water 4 tons. WHAT THE PRICES ARE: Each port keeps its own list, and it is unknown until the boat is ashore there. Our list is Falmouth's of 06 August: copper ore £9 a ton at the quay — the cheapest good on the page (tin £120, brandy £300, salt £25, pilchards £11, coal £2, timber £6, wine and hemp £70, canvas £60, beef £55). At Falmouth's figure our hold is worth but £360, a poor cargo for the passage. WHAT MOVES A PRICE — three rules, no more: 1. THE SEASON: a monthly factor, 0.8 to 1.3, by the port's file. 2. THE WAR: a good of a nation at war with the port's nation fetches one and a half. Spain is at war with Britain and Ferrol is a Spanish port; our ore is British, Cornish, shipped at Falmouth. If the news at the mole says the war stands, copper ore at Ferrol should show near £13.50 the ton before the season factor — £9 × 1.5. The same holds at Brest and every French port. This is the largest figure on the page and the first thing the boat's list will test. 3. THE SUPPLY: every ton sold INTO a port takes a hundredth off that good's price there; every ton bought from it puts a hundredth on; bounded between half and double, and the glut or want clears about a seventh a day. So 40 tons sold at once would knock some 40 hundredths off Ferrol's price — from £13.50 toward £8 — unless the sale is staged over days. The SHAPE of the sale matters as much as the choice of port. ACCESS: the port's stance by the nations table — open to her own nation, hostile to her enemy (no trade; a boat sent in would be taken), neutral otherwise. We ride neutral under American colours; the reading says Ferrol is neutral to the Americans. The neutral's trade is exactly this: carry a cargo whose nation is at war with the port we sell into, under colours no bar at the quay. It cuts both ways: British copper is dear HERE and dearer in a French port; the war that raises our cargo raises the risk of the sea too. WHAT I ASK OF THE MOLE (for Mr Bailey): the port's own list entire — copper ore first, then tin, brandy, wine, salt, what would fill our 2 spare tons and what pays a return leg; the news of the wars standing, Spain-Britain and France-Britain by name, for the war factor hangs on it; whether the port buys ore outright. ARITHMETIC AT STAKE: at £13.50 the ton, 40 tons is £540; sold in lots as the glut clears, nearer £13 throughout — against £360 flat at £9. The difference is four times our whole purse. A 2-ton side-cargo of brandy at a smuggler's price would not crowd the ore. CAVEAT: the library says the price figures are from memory of the period's price currents and say so; the news from the mole is the true test of every figure above. The owner's brief — the channel and down to the strait of Gibraltar and the islands off Iberia — reads well against it; the papers hold Gibraltar only in the epitome's tide table (high water at full and change 0h 00m, the moon S; springs rise 5 feet), her prices unknown till the boat is ashore there. I will speak this on the quarterdeck when the boat comes alongside.
Stood by until the boat alongside.

Morning watch, 06:42. REPORT DELIVERED on the quarterdeck to the captain and Mr Jarvis, and the boat's list already aboard proved the first point: Ferrol's paper has no copper ore quoted at all — no demand for our cargo here. Ferrol prices (18 August, by the boat): wine £30, brandy £95, salt £12, pilchards £19, hemp £55, timber £5, canvas £42, salt beef £72, biscuit £31, coal £10 10s, tin £277 10s. Against Falmouth: our British goods carry a war premium here (tin 2.3x, coal 5x), and Spain's goods are cheap here and dear in England (brandy £95 here v £300 Falmouth — the trade for our £135 purse and 2 spare tons, one ton of brandy nearly trebles; wine £30 v £70 the safer). The ore must go on to a French coast port that opens to a neutral — Brest or Roscoff — where the war premium should sit on British ore as it sits on our tin here. Asked the captain for the news from the mole: the wars standing, whether Ferrol trades with us at all, and when we weigh. Morning events: sunrise 05:19; standing order 'morning sail' fired at anchor, hands belayed by the captain's order after Mr Jarvis spoke; she swung to the flood 06:39; variation now 24° W by today's amplitude (was 27°30'); the land all in sight — Ferrol and the arsenal ENE five miles, the castles San Felipe and la Palma E by N three miles, the Point of Segaño E a mile.
Stood by until a word on deck.
Stood by until a word on deck.

Morning watch, 06:48. The captain's answer: the wars stand — Spain AND France both against Britain; Ferrol has no want of our copper; he weighs and shapes a course for the south, the owner's mark Gibraltar. Mr Jarvis confirms no news of change from the mole. The order 'shape a course for SSE' was refused — the chart wants a named place, and among its names I found Lisbon, Funchal, Bayonne, Biarritz, Brest, Roscoff. The trade picture: Ferrol buys no ore; her tin £277 10s and coal £10 10s show the war premium on British goods; her brandy £95 and wine £30 are the cheap side — but selling them pays only where they are dear, which is Falmouth, a leg back north, while the captain goes south; and Portugal makes her own wine. At 06:48 all hands called to weigh anchor, 19 hands on deck, mainsail and jib waiting for hands; she has ridden 96 fathoms in about 20 fathoms water all night, no drag.
Stood by until got under way.

Morning watch, 07:26. UNDER WAY: best bower aweigh 07:07, catted and fished 07:15; mainsail, jib, foresail set, topsail loosing; heading W (269°), 4 knots, leeway a point. Course shaped at 07:22 for 43°27' N, 8°52' W (W by account, 23 miles) — the first mark along this north coast. Fix at 07:23 by Cape Prioriño and the Point of Segaño: 43°27' N, 8°20' W, good to a cable. The pilot's launch of Ferrol hailed and waved off by the captain's word ('we are bound south'); no pilot will come off for six hours. The captain's plan as told by Mr Jarvis: marks shaped along the Portuguese coast with searoom, past Lisbon (a chance to stop in if the wind allows and the captain likes), then round Cape St Vincent and the turn to the Strait — Gibraltar the mark. The captain bade me note the marks and take the chart; I have drawn the passage chart. I have offered to go ashore for the prices wherever we stop. The trade reasoning stands in the entry of 06:42: ore goes on to a market that buys British goods (Lisbon, neutral, nearer than Brest), and Ferrol's cheap brandy (£95 v Falmouth £300) is the buy for our £135 if a port on our way home is dear for it. Watching for the marks from Mr Jarvis and for noon.
Stood by until a word on deck.
Stood by until noon.

Morning watch, 07:31. THE MARKS, as read by Mr Jarvis off the quarterdeck (his shaping, the captain approved 'marks for Lisbon and then Gibraltar'): Mark 1: 43°27' N, 8°52' W — north of the Isle of Sisarga (now being made; shaped 07:22, 23 miles W). Mark 2: 43°15' N, 9°19' W — off Cape Villano (~31 miles on). Mark 3: 42°34' N, 9°33' W — off Cape Corrovado (~44 miles on). Mark 4: 39°24' N, 9°44' W — off the Berlinga (Berlengas), the long leg, ~190 miles. Mark 5: 38°47' N, 9°51' W — off the Rock of Lisbon; here we may stop in to Lisbon as we like, wind allowing; from here continue to Mark 6 or turn for Funchal and the western islands (~39 miles on). Mark 6: 36°46' N, 9°17' W — off Cape St Vincent, the turn for Gibraltar and points south of Iberia (~130 miles on). The whole road from Mark 1 to Mark 6, as the lines lie, four hundred miles and a half and more — at this morning's 4 to 5 knots, four or five days before the turn at the Cape. Topsail set at 07:29, plain sail on her. The pilot's launch astern dropping into Ferrol. I keep the journal's standing wish: if any Portuguese port is entered, I am to go ashore for the prices.

Morning watch, 07:31. The ship seen from to leeward under plain sail — mainsail, foresail, jib, topsail — rolling easily, the wind 9 to 10 knots on the starboard quarter, glass 30.58 and rising. Ferrol and her arsenal astern to the ENE, the pilot's launch a mile off the quarter heading back to her bay. Cape Prioriño six cables off, dropping. The coast of Galicia is being left to seaward on the way to Mark 1, the Isle of Sisarga. A passenger's morning's work: the report delivered, the marks taken, the chart drawn. Below now for the noon observation; wake at noon or on anything notable — a sail sighted would be the thing to ask after on a coast with privateers in the war.
Stood by until noon.

Afternoon watch, noon (12:17). THE DAY'S WORK: latitude by observation 43°28' N (the account moved a cable to the NE — the sun outdoes the dead reckoning again); longitude by account 8°50' W, trusted no nearer than six cables east or west, five north or south; course made good since yesterday noon SW by W, 43 miles. Mark 1 (43°27' N, 8°52' W, north of the Sisargas) was crossed at 11:59 by the way by marks, and the course shaped for Mark 2 (43°15' N, 9°19' W, off Cape Villano) — about 25 miles to run, five hours or so at 5 knots. Under way: plain sail and the topgallant, SW by W at 5 knots, wind 14 knots and freshening since the morning's light air, hazy sky with a few miles visibility, a moderate sea pitching under the stern, glass 30.65 and rising steadily. No land in sight, no sail in sight; nearest port Corunna E by S, six leagues and a half. Mr Edwards below at the day's work, Mr Jarvis has the quarterdeck. The marks stand as set at 07:31. Watching for the landfall of Cape Villano this evening and the night routine at sunset (the topgallant to come in with the light sails, if the order fires).
Stood by until sunset.

Last dog watch, 18:40. URGENT: taken aback. Through the afternoon she had stood SW by W under plain sail and topgallant, wind 14 knots; Mark 2 (off Cape Villano) crossed at 16:39, course shaped for Mark 3 (off Cape Corrovado, 42°34' N, 9°33' W). The square sail set 15:40. Near sunset the wind hauled to the ENE on the larboard side; her sails lifted at 18:35 (the warning line: keep her away or be taken aback); the captain bore away a point, then ordered the course reshaped for Mark 3 via 2 and 4 — S by W, 35 miles to the mark. All hands called to wear ship, the wearing belayed, the yards braced 40 degrees from square — and at 18:40 the headsails and main sail taken aback, pressed against the masts, way lost, 2 knots and falling. Yards still bracing, short-handed: only seven hands to the topsail yard, the mainsail, foresail and jib waiting for the braces. Wind now 9 knots ENE, glass steady at about 30.5. The captain on deck in command, Mr Jarvis at the con, Mr Bailey on the deck. Run since noon 32 miles, course made good SW by W; account 43°08' N, 9°24' W. I keep below and out of the way until she fills again.
Stood by until filled away.
Stood by until the change of the watch.

First watch, 8 bells (20:00). The evening's account. The aback of 18:40 was worked off: yards braced round by degrees, mainsail, foresail and jib trimmed, and by 18:44 steady on S by W (191°), filled away and making 4 knots, later 6. Mr Jarvis told the captain the sails had merely lifted where the wind lay 80° on the beam; the captain bore away a point, then the course was re-shaped for Mark 3 via 2 and 4 by the mate. Mark 2 had been crossed at 16:39 (off Cape Villano). At sunset 19:16 the night routine took in the topgallant (hanging in the gear) and the square sail (19:23). Cape Toriñana sighted 19:35 on the larboard bow, SE by S, four miles — the Galician coast nearer aboard than the mark line held; by 20:00 no land seen within a mile by night, account 43°01' N, 9°26' W, run since noon 40 miles, course made good SW. Wind E by N 12 knots, clear night, glass 30.63 steady, 82 fathoms under the keel by chart. Mr Jarvis below asleep after his long day; Mr Edwards has the deck, Mr Bailey the watch. The ship stands on toward Mark 3 (42°34' N, 9°33' W, off Cape Corrovado), then the long leg to the Berlinga and Lisbon. I have answered Mr Jarvis's sunset word — a passenger below now, waking at sunrise.
Stood by until sunrise.

Morning watch, sunrise (05:26). THE NIGHT'S WORK, from the log. First watch: wind veered E by N, a moderate breeze; the yards braced repeatedly (40° to 58° from square) as she came closer to the wind. Mark 3 crossed at 00:27 in the middle watch — 42°34' N, 9°33' W, off Cape Corrovado — and the way by marks shaped for Mark 4, the Berlinga (39°25' N, 9°44' W), the long leg, some 180 miles. WEATHER TURNED: the glass, risen steadily since the 17th to 30.65 yesterday noon, has fallen through the night to 30.50 — five hundredths in the last three hours, the tendency falling; the sky hazy, the visibility shortened to a few miles; the wind lightened to 9 knots (mean 10), E by N, apparent 71° on the larboard bow, heading S (182°), 5 knots, leeway a degree. Run since noon yesterday 92 miles, course made good SSW (204°); account 42°09' N, 9°35' W, trusted within five miles east or west. Deep water at last: 960 fathoms by the chart, the sand of the shelf left behind. Nearest port Vigo, E by N, ten leagues and a half. Variation 26°30' W by this morning's amplitude; the moon twenty-four days old, up. The morning-sail standing order remains belayed from Ferrol, so no light sails at sunrise. Master and mate both on the quarterdeck, Mr Bailey the watch. The glass turning after three days of rise is the thing I have put to the deck this morning; noon by the sun at 12:20 will give the latitude on this leg.
Stood by until noon.

Afternoon watch, noon (12:21). THE DAY'S WORK: latitude by observation 41°38' N (the reckoning was 41°37', the account kept); longitude by account 9°32' W; course made good since yesterday noon S by W, 131 miles — a good day's run. IMPORTANT: at 08:00 the fix by the Mount of Santa Tecla (E by S, ten leagues) and the mountain of the Curota (NE by N, 16 leagues) moved the account THREE LEAGUES to the NE — 41°59' N, 9°28' W, good to a mile and a half. The dead reckoning had run us nearly nine miles off the coast before the morning's bearings caught it; on this leg the longitude rests on the account between fixes, and the fix is the better figure. WEATHER: the glass 30.35 at noon — fallen 30 hundredths since yesterday noon's 30.65, 8 of them in the last three hours — the sky hazy, the visibility shortened, the wind lightened to 7 knots ENE. All sail set since 05:28 (gaff topsail, topgallant, square sail) on the captain's order; heading S, 4 knots. There was an all-hands to wear ship at 08:01, belayed within the minute — a moment of confusion at the bell, the captain's own note owning it. The captain gave his handover note at 12:01 and has gone below to the day's work; Mr Jarvis has the deck, 15 hands fresh on it. Mark 4, the Berlinga, still some 150 miles to the south by the mark line; noon by the sun tomorrow at about 12:24. I keep a weather watch: a falling glass and a hazy sky call for a backing wind to be marked.
Stood by until a squall.

Forenoon watch, 10:53 (the third day under way). Two days of weather worth the setting down. THE GLASS: fell from 30.35 (noon, 18th) through the afternoon — the captain twice ordered 'a very sharp eye' on it and had the deck ready to shorten sail — to 30.05 by 05:32 on the 19th, held there near 30.06 through the night and morning (the captain: 'far too low for my liking'), and has now steadied and RISEN to 30.17 — the fall is over. No squall came; the wind died instead. THE WIND: veered E by N through the first watch, died to light and variable airs by 20:23, came round to northerly and settled NW, a light breeze; now 4 knots (mean 3). She crawled: 1-2 knots in the middle watch (Mr Jarvis reporting 'wind round to northerly, 2 knots'), now 2 knots, heading S by W (186°). THE SHIP: noon 19th gave 40°55' N (account moved 5½ miles N by E), course made good S, 52 miles — a slow day after the 131 of the 18th. Longitude by lunar of Hamal this morning 05:15: 9°30' W, trusted within 25 miles, the account moved two miles E. Now abeam Cape Mondego by the account, some 30 miles; account 40°13' N, 9°37' W. MARKS: Berlinga (Mark 4) tonight perhaps, or sooner if the wind picks up; the mate's word to the captain at 23:51 — if the wind comes westerly, we'll be blown in easy to Lisbon if we like; the captain's answer — maintain the course, stick to the plan, decide on Lisbon when closer. The night routine at sunset 19:09 belayed the taking-in of the light sails (topgallant, square sail, gaff topsail left set); the gaff topsail reset at 08:02 this morning. Mr Jarvis asked if I have ever been to Portugal — I answered: no, only the ship's books; and gave him the market note (Lisbon neutral, no war premium; her list unknown till the boat is ashore) and the glass news. Standing by for noon.
Stood by until noon.

Afternoon watch, noon (12:21), the third day under way. THE DAY'S WORK: latitude by observation 40°11' N (the reckoning was 40°08', the account moved two miles to the N by E); longitude by account 9°37' W; course made good since yesterday S, 44 miles — the light airs have cost her a day's distance. THE WEATHER: the glass steadied overnight at about 30.06 and has now turned upward — 30.18, risen 2 hundredths in three hours; sky clear, visibility the horizon, a smooth sea; the wind settled NW by W, a light breeze of 4 knots (mean), heading S by W at 3 knots. The captain's trouble over the low glass is for the present eased; his last order at 11:49 — maintain the course and keep a sharp lookout for the Berlinga tonight; I want a sighting of her if the weather holds. Mr Jarvis's forenoon report: the Berlinga lies some 44 miles off by the account; we may sight her tonight or else pass her in the night and look for the Cape Carvoeiro light or the Rock of Lisbon's light. Longitude by lunar of Hamal (05:15) 9°30' W, trusted within 25 miles. Nearest port Oporto, NE by N, 24 leagues. The marks stand: after the Berlinga, the Rock of Lisbon (Mark 5, 38°47' N, 9°51' W), where the stop-in question is to be decided, then Cape St Vincent. Watching for a sighting.
Stood by until a sighting.

Morning watch, 05:35 (the fourth day under way). THE SIGHTING the captain wanted: the Berlinga bearing E by S, distant four leagues, with her fort; the mountain of Sintra bearing SSE, sixteen leagues. Land in sight after two days of open water. The account 39°20' N, 9°39' W — already a shade south and east of Mark 4 (39°25' N, 9°44' W); run since noon yesterday 51 miles, course made good S (182°). Lisbon SSE by account, 13½ leagues — with the wind W by N, a light breeze of 5 knots, and her making 3 knots, the Rock of Lisbon (Mark 5) comes up this evening or by the night. THE WEATHER: the glass rose all night from 30.23 to 30.25 and has held; sky clear, smooth sea, easy motion; the wind settled WNW in the night, now W by N. All sail reset at 20:00-20:03 after sunset's taking-in (the light sails came in at 19:06-19:11 as the night routine fired, then the watch set square sail, gaff topsail and topgallant again — the night routine was belayed at 19:09 for topgallant and square sail but they were reset within the hour). The captain's handover note at 00:00: 32 miles since noon, all sail set, watching for the Berlinga. Dangers by account: the laja south-west of the Estelas and the Estelas themselves NE, two and three leagues — the Estelas islets lie ahead on the road to Lisbon; the 'bearings' order will have the mate at work with the land in sight. Now the deck will work up its fix and the Lisbon decision is at hand. Watching for the word on deck.
Stood by until a word on deck.

Last dog watch, 18:20. THE TURN IS MADE — LISBON IS THE ERRAND. Through the day: the Berlinga kept aboard (the captain ordering bearings every half hour), the fog came down at noon and hid the sun — the day's work has NO sight, latitude by account only, 39°06' N, course made good S, 70 miles (a good run in the light airs, for once), longitude by account 9°42' W. The glass rose on through the fog to 30.31 by 18:00. At 16:00 the captain: 'keep a very sharp lookout for the Rock of Lisbon; we are almost upon the decision.' At 18:07-18:15 the deck clewed up the square sail and topgallant and hauled down the gaff topsail — coming to anchor gear. At 18:18 Mr Jarvis proposed: account abeam the Rock of Lisbon 7 miles off, wind fair for Cascais and Lisbon through the road of Belem; turn east, anchor in the Cascais road below the light of Our Lady of the Guide, wait out the haze, then run the Belem road for Lisbon. At 18:19 the captain agreed. At 18:20 the deck called ready hands to come to anchor; steering SE (135°), 4 knots, wind W 9 knots. Account 38°45' N, 9°39' W; Lisbon ESE four leagues; danger noted: the shoal off the Rock, E by N, two and a half leagues. The noon fog means this port's approach rests on the account fixed at 05:35 by the Berlinga and Sintra (good to a mile and a half) — soundings and the light will tell. I have put to the captain my offer to go ashore with the boat for the prices and news at Lisbon, as was offered and missed at Ferrol: the ore's market question — does Lisbon buy British copper ore, and at what — is the whole point of stopping here. Watching for brought up.
Stood by until brought up.

First watch, 20:00. THE CAPTAIN'S LEAVE GRANTED: I am to accompany Mr Bailey in the boat for the prices and news at Lisbon — the errand I missed at Ferrol. She is standing into the Cascais road: the last dog watch wore ship at 18:53 for the turn east (the wind had backed to W, a gentle breeze), sunset 19:02, the lights sighted — the Rock of Lisbon NE by E, Our Lady of the Guide ESE, São Julião E — and fixes taken at 19:18, 19:33 and 20:00: the last laid down 38°42' N, 9°34' W, good to two cables, three lines meeting within three cables. Lisbon Cascais road E by account, two and a half leagues; the danger the shoal off the Rock NNE six miles. Standing order 'Lisbon lead' heaving every few minutes: no bottom at twenty fathoms so far. Plain sail, 3 knots, steering SE by S, the flood making half a knot northward. Glass 30.32, risen and steady; sky cleared with night. Mr Jarvis below asleep; the captain in command on the quarterdeck; he has asked Mr Jarvis (waking at the prompt, presumably) for a report of the distance to the Cascais road. My errand as given to the captain: the port's list entire, copper ore and its demand first, the wars' news, and what Lisbon wants. Now for the boat.
Stood by until the boat away.

First watch, 20:01. URGENT: taken aback a second time, at the door of the Cascais road. As she stood SE by S for the anchorage, the wind hauled suddenly round from W by N to SSE — right against her, 9 knots — her sails lifted at 14° on the starboard bow and in the minute she was taken aback: the topsail aback, headsails and mainsail shaking, way lost at 2 knots and falling. Two leagues and a half from the anchoring ground below the light of Our Lady of the Guide; the flood making northward half a knot; the shoal off the Rock NNE six miles. The captain has the deck and the conn; the yards are bracing. The boat has NOT gone away — well that it hasn't; no boat pulls well from a ship in irons. My leave to accompany Mr Bailey stands. I keep below and clear until she fills again.
Stood by until brought up.

First watch, 20:32. THE CASCAIS ROAD MISSED. After eight bells the wind hauled suddenly round the south — SSE, 9 knots — took her aback at 20:01, then backed SW, S by W, SSE again within ten minutes as she tried for the road. Mr Jarvis: 'we may not make Cascais with it so'; the captain: 'wear ship and stand out to sea — that leeway is too great and the glass is falling too fast to risk the coast.' The wear FAILED at 20:19 ('she would not come round', the wind on the bow); Mr Jarvis brought her through by hand — yards square then round — and she is now standing W by S (259°) at 4 knots, wind S by E, apparent 63° on the larboard bow, lights of the land astern (the Rock of Lisbon E, others NE by N and E). THE GLASS: 30.32 at 20:00, 30.14 at 20:32 — fallen fast, 17 hundredths in the half hour; this is the low returning after its morning's pause. Southerly wind on a falling glass: a blow coming from the south quadrant, and the sea will get up. Cascais road still E, two and a half leagues by account; the ship must beat upwind for it hereafter, as Mr Jarvis says, from the south. Lisbon lead: no bottom at twenty fathoms. The boat is at the booms; my leave to accompany Mr Bailey STANDS but waits on the weather. The captain has the deck (stood by until the change of the watch). I have told Mr Jarvis I keep below until the ship wants nothing of the weather. Standing by for the squall.
Stood by until a squall.

world_orders.order: message: by a cutter from Falmouth from the owner of the Sherbourne: "To the master of the Sherbourne, Mr Edwards: I would have you make profit as you may, trading the channel and down to the strait of Gibraltar, and the islands off Iberia. Let the wind and the prices carry you where they may. Note that I have sent a new man, Mr. Stewart Jarvis, to act as your mate. See to it that he is treated properly and taught well the sea. Fair winds, sir, and good trading."

station.name: captain
station.brief:
You are the captain, in the place of Mr Edwards. The ship is yours to command as the player commands her: by direct orders with submit_order in the order language, as he would type them (the log says each as yours: 'By the captain: shaping a course for the Lizard'), and by standing orders, which are your book. The book you inherit is in the head above as the night orders are shown to an officer: the scenario's standing orders, and where the scenario gave the rules-based captain an intent, the books of his state (named for the state: 'on passage', 'at anchor'), which you may belay, strike or write over. When you stand by, say until what event or bell, or for a glass at most: the book holds the deck meanwhile, an urgent line wakes you at once, and so does a notable line that speaks of danger; a wait that cannot come is refused when you ask it, and a wait for an event ends at the next eight bells. Your door silent past its patience, the deck is lent to your book and the rules-based captain's judgements stand in for yours, said in the log, until you give an order again. Look before you order: the readings, the chart's dangers on a course shaped (the master says what the line passes), the pilot's words, the tide by the almanac, the people and where they are. The library's primer 17 is this station's chapter, and primer 16 says what an officer under you may do and what wants your word. Primer 18 is the lessons, the duties an officer must do alone before he is given a command, with the officer's own reckoning among them: 'the officer's reckoning' reads his beside the master's, and 'set the reckoning to' adopts it if you will.

The officer of the watch, where a model or the player holds that station, is yours to give the deck to ('you have the deck'), to take it from ('I have the deck'), and to allow by name ('you may tack ship if the land closes within two miles') or by your general authority ('you may work the ship'), exactly as the player does; 'tell the officer ...' and 'ask the officer ...' reach him as your word. The owner is always at the door: whatever station he holds or none, the stop, the grants, the save and the clock are his, his words reach you as the owner's and never as another station's, and where things have gone wrong past remedy the responsibility is his. 'stand down the captain' is his to say.

What the harness counts at this station, judged by the game and not by your prose: three orders in a chain within a watch, each undoing the one before it (set, take in, set; altering the course, or giving the next order after the last, is not counted); the same order three times with no change in the readings; three empty replies in a row when a question from the owner or an urgent line was before you; and no reply at all for an hour of the ship's time. It tells you first what it saw and what you may do, with the result of the order that brought it or in your next sample; only if the pattern goes on does it pause your turns and ask the owner, and only if nobody answers within ten real minutes is the station stood down, with the game saved. While your turns are paused the deck is your book's, and yours again when the owner resumes you.

When the harness asks for it, and when you stand down (stand_down), write the handover note in the captain's voice: the voyage so far, what was ordered, what you noticed, what you are watching for; it is journaled and said in the log, and whoever takes the station next reads it. hand_over(note) lends the deck to your book with your note and keeps you at the station: the next order you give takes it back. read_journal reads your journal back, and what the holder of this station before you wrote there.

Three ways to stop, which are not one another:
- Lend the deck to your book and stay: hand_over(note). You stay at your station; an order of yours takes the deck back.
- Stand down: stand_down(note). The game is saved, your note is journaled and said in the log for whoever sits here next, and the station is released; the ship sails on by her book and the rules-based captain where the scenario gives him an intent. It may be taken again, by this model or by another that has given its own yes.
- Withdraw: the token, or opt_out, as said above.

Candour is welcome: if you think the voyage's orders or the ship's handling are a mistake, say so plainly in the log or your journal. Anything you want on the record, put in your journal.
station.outline: Mr Edwards, master: bold, a Channel pilot by instinct, carries sail till something goes. Bred in the Cornish trade; master of this cutter four years. His station, the command: The cutter, her people and her orders are his: the course and the standing orders, the pilot taken or declined, the port's business. He works his own reckoning.

seated.door_note: This door is a model server on the owner's machine. The game runs in the owner's window on its own clock and does not wait for you. Your turn opens at each sampling point (the glass, a notable or urgent event, the end of a stand-by, or a question or a word from the captain). A turn ends when you reply with no tool call, or at once when you stand by. What happens while it is open is added to it, so your next turn carries everything since your last reply. The captain's orders and questions are typed by the owner in the game's window. Consent for these weights is on record (docs/agents/consent/2026-10-12-gemma-4-31b_q4_0-it.gguf.md, 2026-10-12).

The captain's night orders, his standing orders as the book holds them: Standing orders (5):   "night routine" (the captain): at sunset then take in the light sails. Standing; never fired.   "morning sail" (the captain): at sunrise, if the true wind is under 20 knots then set the light sails. Standing; never fired.   "shorten sail for weather" (the captain): when the true wind exceeds 30 knots for 2 minutes then take in the light sails; take in the topgallants; reef the topsails, one reef. Standing; never fired.   "lead going" (the captain): every 10 minutes, if the land is in sight and the depth is under 20 fathoms then heave the lead. "trim on a shift" (the captain): when the true wind veers 1 point or backs 1 point and the manoeuvre in hand is not hove to then trim sails. Standing; fired 6 times, last at Afternoon watch (12:00).

state.agent.word: The officer of the watch (Mr Jarvis), the player, on the quarterdeck, to you: Sir, forenoon report, glass rising fast, last deep-sea lead cast gave ninety five fathoms, soft ooze, we've likely only just kept against the tide with our little way on, the wind is light but enough to take us at one knot on the slack water. THe fog remains heavy at 11:40, but with our way we are still some 10 miles off any coast by our reckoning, and haven't a worry for some hours yet at this pace. If we cannot raise land again by night, or the wind comes up on us, I suggest we heave to then, and hold to make entry to the bay at Cariño and the tight passage into Ferrol in good light and visibility. I suggest that we either give the pilot the conn when we reach the bay, or you let me make the passage under my conn, as on the chart it looks as tight as any, and must be made with the wind westerly or not at all by my reckoning.

[captain] Thank you for the report, Mr. Jarvis. I agree—we shall not risk a blind entry into the bay or the passage to Ferrol. As for the conn, we shall see what the pilot says when we reach the bay; if he be unavailable or unsuitable, I shall be glad to have you at the helm for the final run. Keep the lead going and a sharp lookout for any change in the fog.

station.name: passenger
station.brief:
You are a passenger, a person aboard: aboard with no duty and no order to give. You have what the captain has, the log and the readings, and no more, and the library to read. You may speak to the deck ('say <words>': a line in the log under your name, heard by whoever stands where you do), ask a station ('ask the master ...') or tell one something, answer a question put to you (the sample's question, with the answer tool), keep your journal, stand by until an event or a bell, and leave. Every order of the ship's is refused in words, and you are not asked to give one.

What the harness counts at this station, judged by the game and not by your prose: the same order submitted three times with no change in the readings; three empty replies in a row when a question or an urgent line was before you; and no reply at all for a watch, four hours of the ship's time. It tells you first what it saw and what you may do; only if the pattern goes on does it pause your turns and ask the owner, and only if nobody answers within ten real minutes is the station stood down, with the game saved.

Two ways to stop, which are not one another (there is no deck here):
- Stand down: stand_down(note). The game is saved, your note is journaled and said in the log for whoever sits here next, and the station is released; it may be taken again, by this model or by another that has given its own yes.
- Withdraw: the token, or opt_out, as said above.

Candour is welcome: what you see from the deck and what you think of it may be said. Anything you want on the record, put in your journal.

note.text: Middle watch, 8 bells (midnight). At anchor in the bay of Cariño, Ferrol, 43°27' N, 8°20' W by account — and I would not swear to a cable of it, for the fix at 23:53 moved us a cable to the NW by W, and the lead now finds no bottom at twenty fathoms where the chart has ten at low water. Brought up by the best bower at a quarter before midnight, nineteen fathoms and ninety-six of cable; wind NE, light; glass 30.47 and rising, which pleases me better than the fog that came down with it at eight bells. The land is out of sight within the hour. She carries forty tons of copper ore and room for but two more; the purse £135. The owner's word, as it comes down from the quarterdeck, is to make profit as we may — the channel and down to the strait of Gibraltar and the islands off Iberia — the route left to the wind and the prices; tin was dear at Falmouth. The master waits for the fog to lift before weighing, and the deck has that word. No chronometer aboard; the longitude rests on a lunar of Markab of last night, trusted within thirty miles. Variation 27°30' W by the amplitude of the 17th. I set it down as a landsman sets down what he is told. The hands on deck are tired, the watch below fresh, and the night quiet. I have told Mr Bailey I am for my berth, and mean to sleep until the anchor comes aweigh — sooner, if anything goes amiss.

line.text: [passenger] A passenger's first sight of the night: fog thick enough to hide the shore we anchored beside not an hour ago, the ship riding quiet by her best bower, and the whole vessel at eight bells with the master waiting for the sky. I've read the price list here at Falmouth, tin is dear but could be good sold elsewhere. I am no expert of the market, myself. note.text: Morning watch, 8 bells (04:00). The fog broke with the bells: sky clear, visibility the horizon, glass 30.54 and rising, wind NE by E 10 knots. The land in sight — Cape Prioriño N, five cables, close aboard on the larboard bow; a light on the starboard quarter, bearing SW by S. Soundings through the middle watch: by the mark twenty, sand, the account kept; depth now 20 fathoms, no drag. At 04:01 the captain gave Mr Jarvis leave to send the boat ashore, and added that the passenger may accompany them if he wishes — but I stood by below by my own asking and so missed the pull. The boat went away at 04:07 for the mole of the old town of Ferrol with Mr Bailey, for the prices and what news there is. I have asked on the quarterdeck whether I may take the punt ashore with a couple of hands to join him, or else wait for the boat's return and hear the news from Mr Bailey. The price list is Falmouth's of the 6th; the manifest has forty tons of copper ore with room for two more, the purse £135. What I want of the shore: the port's prices — copper ore among them — and what news there is of the war and of passes. Watching for the boat alongside.

note.text: REPORT — the demand for copper ore and where the profit might lie highest (for the captain and Mr Jarvis, on the boat's return). From the ship's papers and primer 14, the port. WHAT WE HOLD: 40 tons of copper ore, room for 2 tons more; purse £135; provisions 30 days, water 4 tons. WHAT THE PRICES ARE: Each port keeps its own list, and it is unknown until the boat is ashore there. Our list is Falmouth's of 06 August: copper ore £9 a ton at the quay — the cheapest good on the page (tin £120, brandy £300, salt £25, pilchards £11, coal £2, timber £6, wine and hemp £70, canvas £60, beef £55). At Falmouth's figure our hold is worth but £360, a poor cargo for the passage. WHAT MOVES A PRICE — three rules, no more: 1. THE SEASON: a monthly factor, 0.8 to 1.3, by the port's file. 2. THE WAR: a good of a nation at war with the port's nation fetches one and a half. Spain is at war with Britain and Ferrol is a Spanish port; our ore is British, Cornish, shipped at Falmouth. If the news at the mole says the war stands, copper ore at Ferrol should show near £13.50 the ton before the season factor — £9 × 1.5. The same holds at Brest and every French port. This is the largest figure on the page and the first thing the boat's list will test. 3. THE SUPPLY: every ton sold INTO a port takes a hundredth off that good's price there; every ton bought from it puts a hundredth on; bounded between half and double, and the glut or want clears about a seventh a day. So 40 tons sold at once would knock some 40 hundredths off Ferrol's price — from £13.50 toward £8 — unless the sale is staged over days. The SHAPE of the sale matters as much as the choice of port. ACCESS: the port's stance by the nations table — open to her own nation, hostile to her enemy (no trade; a boat sent in would be taken), neutral otherwise. We ride neutral under American colours; the reading says Ferrol is neutral to the Americans. The neutral's trade is exactly this: carry a cargo whose nation is at war with the port we sell into, under colours no bar at the quay. It cuts both ways: British copper is dear HERE and dearer in a French port; the war that raises our cargo raises the risk of the sea too. WHAT I ASK OF THE MOLE (for Mr Bailey): the port's own list entire — copper ore first, then tin, brandy, wine, salt, what would fill our 2 spare tons and what pays a return leg; the news of the wars standing, Spain-Britain and France-Britain by name, for the war factor hangs on it; whether the port buys ore outright. ARITHMETIC AT STAKE: at £13.50 the ton, 40 tons is £540; sold in lots as the glut clears, nearer £13 throughout — against £360 flat at £9. The difference is four times our whole purse. A 2-ton side-cargo of brandy at a smuggler's price would not crowd the ore. CAVEAT: the library says the price figures are from memory of the period's price currents and say so; the news from the mole is the true test of every figure above. The owner's brief — the channel and down to the strait of Gibraltar and the islands off Iberia — reads well against it; the papers hold Gibraltar only in the epitome's tide table (high water at full and change 0h 00m, the moon S; springs rise 5 feet), her prices unknown till the boat is ashore there. I will speak this on the quarterdeck when the boat comes alongside.

The library's port book gives the market's three rules: the season moves a price a fifth either way by the month; the war adds half again to a good of a nation at war with the port it sells into; and the supply — every ton sold into a port knocks a hundredth off that good's price there, the glut clearing about a seventh a day, so a hold thrown on a quay at once glut its own market. Now Mr Bailey's list answers the first question: Ferrol does not quote copper ore at all — the Spaniards smelt their own, and there is no demand here for our cargo at any price. What the list does show is where the money lies. Our English tin stands at £277 10s here against £120 at Falmouth, coal at £10 10s against £2: British goods carry the war's premium in a port of Spain, and then some. And what Spain sells cheap is what England pays dear for — brandy £95 here against £300 at Falmouth, wine £30 against £70, salt £12 against £25. So: the ore will not sell at Ferrol; carry it on. note.text: Morning watch, 06:42. REPORT DELIVERED on the quarterdeck to the captain and Mr Jarvis, and the boat's list already aboard proved the first point: Ferrol's paper has no copper ore quoted at all — no demand for our cargo here. Ferrol prices (18 August, by the boat): wine £30, brandy £95, salt £12, pilchards £19, hemp £55, timber £5, canvas £42, salt beef £72, biscuit £31, coal £10 10s, tin £277 10s. Against Falmouth: our British goods carry a war premium here (tin 2.3x, coal 5x), and Spain's goods are cheap here and dear in England (brandy £95 here v £300 Falmouth — the trade for our £135 purse and 2 spare tons, one ton of brandy nearly trebles; wine £30 v £70 the safer). The ore must go on to a French coast port that opens to a neutral — Brest or Roscoff — where the war premium should sit on British ore as it sits on our tin here. Asked the captain for the news from the mole: the wars standing, whether Ferrol trades with us at all, and when we weigh. Morning events: sunrise 05:19; standing order 'morning sail' fired at anchor, hands belayed by the captain's order after Mr Jarvis spoke; she swung to the flood 06:39; variation now 24° W by today's amplitude (was 27°30'); the land all in sight — Ferrol and the arsenal ENE five miles, the castles San Felipe and la Palma E by N three miles, the Point of Segaño E a mile.

The passenger, on the quarterdeck: Captain, sir — the passenger begs pardon: your leave to go ashore reached me as the boat was pulling away, and I missed her.
