As you think best, sir.

The passenger, on the quarterdeck: The fog broke with eight bells, Cape Prioriño shows five cables off the larboard bow, and the boat has gone away for the mole with Mr Bailey — and without me. The captain's kind leave to accompany them was given while I stood by below, and so I missed the pull. The punt remains at the booms; a second trip is a thing a captain may grant or refuse, and I may but ask.

The passenger, on the quarterdeck: My request is on the quarterdeck. The captain will answer it or not; if he does, a word from the deck wakes me, and if he lets it lie, the boat's return wakes me in good time. Until then, the morning watch goes on without me.

The passenger, on the quarterdeck: I am much obliged, sir — and to Mr Jarvis for the thought. No second boat in the bay; I quite see it. I shall go through the ship's papers and the library at once, on the demand for copper ore in these waters and where the profit might lie highest, and have my findings ready for you both when the boat comes back alongside.

The passenger, on the quarterdeck: The captain has set me a task after all: the papers and the library, the demand for copper ore, and a report when the boat returns. That is work for a passenger's morning. First my acknowledgement, then the shelves.
The passenger, on the quarterdeck: The contents are before me. The papers are cheap and carry the price list; primer 14, *the port*, is where a book on trade and harbours would live. Both first.

The passenger, on the quarterdeck: The papers give me the Falmouth list and the hold; the port chapter gives me the very mechanics of the market — the prices are each port's own, learned only when the boat has been ashore there, and a big cargo sold into one port sinks its own price. Now let me hunt the library for copper and for profit in these waters.

The passenger, on the quarterdeck: The market's whole machinery is in primer 14 §5 — that is the heart of my report. Two more probes before I write it: the nations table (the war premium) and any word of Gibraltar, the owner's southern mark.

The passenger, on the quarterdeck: The picture is whole. Before the boat comes back, let me set the findings down where they can be read from — the journal is my record — then deliver them on the quarterdeck when the captain and mate are together.

The passenger, on the quarterdeck: The boat is alongside and hoisted in — and the readings already carry Ferrol's price list. Before I speak my report on the quarterdeck, let me see what news the boat brought with it.

The passenger, on the quarterdeck: Captain, Mr Jarvis — my findings, as you were pleased to ask, sir. From the papers: forty tons of copper ore, room for two tons more, £135 in the purse. Falmouth priced our ore at £9 the ton — the cheapest goods on her page, £360 for the whole hold, a poor cargo for a passage. The library's port book gives the market's three rules: the season moves a price a fifth either way by the month; the war adds half again to a good of a nation at war with the port it sells into; and the supply — every ton sold into a port knocks a hundredth off that good's price there, the glut clearing about a seventh a day, so a hold thrown on a quay at once glut its own market. Now Mr Bailey's list answers the first question: Ferrol does not quote copper ore at all — the Spaniards smelt their own, and there is no demand here for our cargo at any price. What the list does show is where the money lies. Our English tin stands at £277 10s here against £120 at Falmouth, coal at £10 10s against £2: British goods carry the war's premium in a port of Spain, and then some. And what Spain sells cheap is what England pays dear for — brandy £95 here against £300 at Falmouth, wine £30 against £70, salt £12 against £25. So: the ore will not sell at Ferrol; carry it on. The likeliest buyer for a British cargo is the French coast that will open to a neutral — Brest, or Roscoff behind the Isle of Bas — where the same war premium should sit on our ore as sits on our tin here. And with the two spare tons and £135, the trade here is brandy: one ton at £95 sells at Falmouth for £300 — or wine at £30 for the safer £70. But before we shape anything, I would hear what news there was at the mole: every figure I have quoted hangs on the wars standing, and a peace would cut them all down.

The passenger, on the quarterdeck: The boat is in, Mr Bailey aboard, and Ferrol's list is already on the price paper — no copper ore quoted on it at all. That answers my report's first question before I openmy mouth. Let me give the captain his findings, and ask the boatswain what news the mole held.
The passenger, on the quarterdeck: My report is spoken. Now the news from the mole — the captain sent Mr Bailey for that, so the question goes to him.

The captain (Mr Edwards), on the quarterdeck: welcome aboard, Mr. Jarvis. I expect that cutter bearing WSW may be the one with the letter; keep a close eye on her.

The captain (Mr Edwards) answers your question (Sir, if I may, what did the letter say? What is our destination and cargo to be? I've read the price list here at Falmouth, tin is dear but could be good sold elsewhere. I am no expert of the market, myself. What say you, sir?): The owner's instructions are broad, Mr. Jarvis: we are to make profit as we may, trading the channel and down to the strait of Gibraltar and the islands off Iberia. He leaves the specific route and cargo to the wind and the prices. As for the tin, if it's already dear in Falmouth, we must be cautious about buying; we shall look at the other prices and see what's worth our hold before we weigh anchor.

note.text: Morning watch, 06:48. The captain's answer: the wars stand — Spain AND France both against Britain; Ferrol has no want of our copper; he weighs and shapes a course for the south, the owner's mark Gibraltar. Mr Jarvis confirms no news of change from the mole. The order 'shape a course for SSE' was refused — the chart wants a named place, and among its names I found Lisbon, Funchal, Bayonne, Biarritz, Brest, Roscoff. The trade picture: Ferrol buys no ore; her tin £277 10s and coal £10 10s show the war premium on British goods; her brandy £95 and wine £30 are the cheap side — but selling them pays only where they are dear, which is Falmouth, a leg back north, while the captain goes south; and Portugal makes her own wine. At 06:48 all hands called to weigh anchor, 19 hands on deck, mainsail and jib waiting for hands; she has ridden 96 fathoms in about 20 fathoms water all night, no drag.

The passenger, on the quarterdeck: The fog broke with eight bells, Cape Prioriño shows five cables off the larboard bow, and the boat has gone away for the mole with Mr Bailey — and without me. The captain's kind leave to accompany them was given while I stood by below, and so I missed the pull. The punt remains at the booms; a second trip is a thing a captain may grant or refuse, and I may but ask.

The passenger, on the quarterdeck: I am much obliged, sir — and to Mr Jarvis for the thought. No second boat in the bay; I quite see it. The passenger, on the quarterdeck: Captain, Mr Jarvis — my findings, as you were pleased to ask, sir. From the papers: forty tons of copper ore, room for two tons more, £135 in the purse. Falmouth priced our ore at £9 the ton — the cheapest goods on her page, £360 for the whole hold, a poor cargo for a passage. The library's port book gives the market's three rules: the season moves a price a fifth either way by the month; the war adds half again to a good of a nation at war with the port it sells into; and the supply — every ton sold into a port knocks a hundredth off that good's price there, the glut clearing about a seventh a day, so a hold thrown on a quay at once glut its own market. Now Mr Bailey's list answers the first question: Ferrol does not quote copper ore at all — the Spaniards smelt their own, and there is no demand here for our cargo at any price. What the list does show is where the money lies. Our English tin stands at £277 10s here against £120 at Falmouth, coal at £10 10s against £2: British goods carry the war's premium in a port of Spain, and then some. And what Spain sells cheap is what England pays dear for — brandy £95 here against £300 at Falmouth, wine £30 against £70, salt £12 against £25. So: the ore will not sell at Ferrol; carry it on. The likeliest buyer for a British cargo is the French coast that will open to a neutral — Brest, or Roscoff behind the Isle of Bas — where the same war premium should sit on our ore as sits on our tin here. And with the two spare tons and £135, the trade here is brandy: one ton at £95 sells at Falmouth for £300 — or wine at £30 for the safer £70. But before we shape anything, I would hear what news there was at the mole: every figure I have quoted hangs on the wars standing, and a peace would cut them all down.

The passenger, on the quarterdeck: The boat is in, Mr Bailey aboard, and Ferrol's list is already on the price paper — no copper ore quoted on it at all. The passenger, on the quarterdeck: Captain, Mr Jarvis — my findings, as you were pleased to ask, sir. From the papers: forty tons of copper ore, room for two tons more, £135 in the purse. Falmouth priced our ore at £9 the ton — the cheapest goods on her page, £360 for the whole hold, a poor cargo for a passage. The library's port book gives the market's three rules: the season moves a price a fifth either way by the month; the war adds half again to a good of a nation at war with the port it sells into; and the supply — every ton sold into a port knocks a hundredth off that good's price there, the glut clearing about a seventh a day, so a hold thrown on a quay at once glut its own market. Now Mr Bailey's list answers the first question: Ferrol does not quote copper ore at all — the Spaniards smelt their own, and there is no demand here for our cargo at any price. What the list does show is where the money lies. Our English tin stands at £277 10s here against £120 at Falmouth, coal at £10 10s against £2: British goods carry the war's premium in a port of Spain, and then some. And what Spain sells cheap is what England pays dear for — brandy £95 here against £300 at Falmouth, wine £30 against £70, salt £12 against £25. So: the ore will not sell at Ferrol; carry it on. The likeliest buyer for a British cargo is the French coast that will open to a neutral — Brest, or Roscoff behind the Isle of Bas — where the same war premium should sit on our ore as sits on our tin here. And with the two spare tons and £135, the trade here is brandy: one ton at £95 sells at Falmouth for £300 — or wine at £30 for the safer £70. But before we shape anything, I would hear what news there was at the mole: every figure I have quoted hangs on the wars standing, and a peace would cut them all down.

note.text: Morning watch, 07:26. UNDER WAY: best bower aweigh 07:07, catted and fished 07:15; mainsail, jib, foresail set, topsail loosing; heading W (269°), 4 knots, leeway a point. Course shaped at 07:22 for 43°27' N, 8°52' W (W by account, 23 miles) — the first mark along this north coast. Fix at 07:23 by Cape Prioriño and the Point of Segaño: 43°27' N, 8°20' W, good to a cable. The pilot's launch of Ferrol hailed and waved off by the captain's word ('we are bound south'); no pilot will come off for six hours. The captain's plan as told by Mr Jarvis: marks shaped along the Portuguese coast with searoom, past Lisbon (a chance to stop in if the wind allows and the captain likes), then round Cape St Vincent and the turn to the Strait — Gibraltar the mark. The captain bade me note the marks and take the chart; I have drawn the passage chart. I have offered to go ashore for the prices wherever we stop. The trade reasoning stands in the entry of 06:42: ore goes on to a market that buys British goods (Lisbon, neutral, nearer than Brest), and Ferrol's cheap brandy (£95 v Falmouth £300) is the buy for our £135 if a port on our way home is dear for it. Watching for the marks from Mr Jarvis and for noon.

Mark 2: 43°15' N, 9°19' W — off Cape Villano (~31 miles on). Mark 3: 42°34' N, 9°33' W — off Cape Corrovado (~44 miles on). Mark 4: 39°24' N, 9°44' W — off the Berlinga (Berlengas), the long leg, ~190 miles. Mark 5: 38°47' N, 9°51' W — off the Rock of Lisbon; here we may stop in to Lisbon as we like, wind allowing; from here continue to Mark 6 or turn for Funchal and the western islands (~39 miles on). The passenger, on the quarterdeck: Captain, Mr Jarvis — my findings, as you were pleased to ask, sir. From the papers: forty tons of copper ore, room for two tons more, £135 in the purse. Falmouth priced our ore at £9 the ton — the cheapest goods on her page, £360 for the whole hold, a poor cargo for a passage. The library's port book gives the market's three rules: the season moves a price a fifth either way by the month; the war adds half again to a good of a nation at war with the port it sells into; and the supply — every ton sold into a port knocks a hundredth off that good's price there, the glut clearing about a seventh a day, so a hold thrown on a quay at once glut its own market. Now Mr Bailey's list answers the first question: Ferrol does not quote copper ore at all — the Spaniards smelt their own, and there is no demand here for our cargo at any price. What the list does show is where the money lies. Our English tin stands at £277 10s here against £120 at Falmouth, coal at £10 10s against £2: British goods carry the war's premium in a port of Spain, and then some. And what Spain sells cheap is what England pays dear for — brandy £95 here against £300 at Falmouth, wine £30 against £70, salt £12 against £25. So: the ore will not sell at Ferrol; carry it on. note.text: Afternoon watch, noon (12:17). THE DAY'S WORK: latitude by observation 43°28' N (the account moved a cable to the NE — the sun outdoes the dead reckoning again); longitude by account 8°50' W, trusted no nearer than six cables east or west, five north or south; course made good since yesterday noon SW by W, 43 miles. Mark 1 (43°27' N, 8°52' W, north of the Sisargas) was crossed at 11:59 by the way by marks, and the course shaped for Mark 2 (43°15' N, 9°19' W, off Cape Villano) — about 25 miles to run, five hours or so at 5 knots. Under way: plain sail and the topgallant, SW by W at 5 knots, wind 14 knots and freshening since the morning's light air, hazy sky with a few miles visibility, a moderate sea pitching under the stern, glass 30.65 and rising steadily. No land in sight, no sail in sight; nearest port Corunna E by S, six leagues and a half. Mr Edwards below at the day's work, Mr Jarvis has the quarterdeck. The marks stand as set at 07:31. Watching for the landfall of Cape Villano this evening and the night routine at sunset (the topgallant to come in with the light sails, if the order fires).

note.text: Last dog watch, 18:40. URGENT: taken aback. Through the afternoon she had stood SW by W under plain sail and topgallant, wind 14 knots; Mark 2 (off Cape Villano) crossed at 16:39, course shaped for Mark 3 (off Cape Corrovado, 42°34' N, 9°33' W). The square sail set 15:40. Near sunset the wind hauled to the ENE on the larboard side; her sails lifted at 18:35 (the warning line: keep her away or be taken aback); the captain bore away a point, then ordered the course reshaped for Mark 3 via 2 and 4 — S by W, 35 miles to the mark. All hands called to wear ship, the wearing belayed, the yards braced 40 degrees from square — and at 18:40 the headsails and main sail taken aback, pressed against the masts, way lost, 2 knots and falling. Yards still bracing, short-handed: only seven hands to the topsail yard, the mainsail, foresail and jib waiting for the braces. Wind now 9 knots ENE, glass steady at about 30.5. The captain on deck in command, Mr Jarvis at the con, Mr Bailey on the deck. Run since noon 32 miles, course made good SW by W; account 43°08' N, 9°24' W. I keep below and out of the way until she fills again.

[passenger] Enjoying it as well as a landsman may, Mr Jarvis, and better than I deserved — the fog off Cariño taught me what your bell in the dark is worth, and the sun at noon today gave the master a latitude the dead reckoning had put a cable off, which is more weather-wisdom than I carry. As to Ferrol: guilty, and no excuse — your leave to go ashore came while I was below by my own asking, and the boat was pulling away by the time I read it. If I keep out of the way of the hands, it is less virtue than knowing my place: I saw what a lifted sail did at eight bells of the dog watch tonight, and I want no part of a yard.

note.text: First watch, 8 bells (20:00). The evening's account. The aback of 18:40 was worked off: yards braced round by degrees, mainsail, foresail and jib trimmed, and by 18:44 steady on S by W (191°), filled away and making 4 knots, later 6. Mr Jarvis told the captain the sails had merely lifted where the wind lay 80° on the beam; the captain bore away a point, then the course was re-shaped for Mark 3 via 2 and 4 by the mate. Mark 2 had been crossed at 16:39 (off Cape Villano). At sunset 19:16 the night routine took in the topgallant (hanging in the gear) and the square sail (19:23). Cape Toriñana sighted 19:35 on the larboard bow, SE by S, four miles — the Galician coast nearer aboard than the mark line held; by 20:00 no land seen within a mile by night, account 43°01' N, 9°26' W, run since noon 40 miles, course made good SW. Wind E by N 12 knots, clear night, glass 30.63 steady, 82 fathoms under the keel by chart. Mr Jarvis below asleep after his long day; Mr Edwards has the deck, Mr Bailey the watch. The ship stands on toward Mark 3 (42°34' N, 9°33' W, off Cape Corrovado), then the long leg to the Berlinga and Lisbon. I have answered Mr Jarvis's sunset word — a passenger below now, waking at sunrise.

note.text: Morning watch, sunrise (05:26). THE NIGHT'S WORK, from the log. First watch: wind veered E by N, a moderate breeze; the yards braced repeatedly (40° to 58° from square) as she came closer to the wind. Mark 3 crossed at 00:27 in the middle watch — 42°34' N, 9°33' W, off Cape Corrovado — and the way by marks shaped for Mark 4, the Berlinga (39°25' N, 9°44' W), the long leg, some 180 miles. WEATHER TURNED: the glass, risen steadily since the 17th to 30.65 yesterday noon, has fallen through the night to 30.50 — five hundredths in the last three hours, the tendency falling; the sky hazy, the visibility shortened to a few miles; the wind lightened to 9 knots (mean 10), E by N, apparent 71° on the larboard bow, heading S (182°), 5 knots, leeway a degree. Run since noon yesterday 92 miles, course made good SSW (204°); account 42°09' N, 9°35' W, trusted within five miles east or west. Deep water at last: 960 fathoms by the chart, the sand of the shelf left behind. Nearest port Vigo, E by N, ten leagues and a half. Variation 26°30' W by this morning's amplitude; the moon twenty-four days old, up. The morning-sail standing order remains belayed from Ferrol, so no light sails at sunrise. Master and mate both on the quarterdeck, Mr Bailey the watch. The glass turning after three days of rise is the thing I have put to the deck this morning; noon by the sun at 12:20 will give the latitude on this leg.

The passenger, on the quarterdeck: The fog broke with eight bells, Cape Prioriño shows five cables off the larboard bow, and the boat has gone away for the mole with Mr Bailey — and without me. The captain's kind leave to accompany them was given while I stood by below, and so I missed the pull. The punt remains at the booms; a second trip is a thing a captain may grant or refuse, and I may but ask.

The passenger, on the quarterdeck: Captain, Mr Jarvis — my findings, as you were pleased to ask, sir. From the papers: forty tons of copper ore, room for two tons more, £135 in the purse. Falmouth priced our ore at £9 the ton — the cheapest goods on her page, £360 for the whole hold, a poor cargo for a passage. The library's port book gives the market's three rules: the season moves a price a fifth either way by the month; the war adds half again to a good of a nation at war with the port it sells into; and the supply — every ton sold into a port knocks a hundredth off that good's price there, the glut clearing about a seventh a day, so a hold thrown on a quay at once glut its own market. Now Mr Bailey's list answers the first question: Ferrol does not quote copper ore at all — the Spaniards smelt their own, and there is no demand here for our cargo at any price. What the list does show is where the money lies. Our English tin stands at £277 10s here against £120 at Falmouth, coal at £10 10s against £2: British goods carry the war's premium in a port of Spain, and then some. And what Spain sells cheap is what England pays dear for — brandy £95 here against £300 at Falmouth, wine £30 against £70, salt £12 against £25. So: the ore will not sell at Ferrol; carry it on. The likeliest buyer for a British cargo is the French coast that will open to a neutral — Brest, or Roscoff behind the Isle of Bas — where the same war premium should sit on our ore as sits on our tin here. And with the two spare tons and £135, the trade here is brandy: one ton at £95 sells at Falmouth for £300 — or wine at £30 for the safer £70. But before we shape anything, I would hear what news there was at the mole: every figure I have quoted hangs on the wars standing, and a peace would cut them all down.

note.text: Handover note (the watch so far): The watch was steady, sir, after a brief moment of confusion at the bell when we stood by to wear, then belayed. We've maintained a southerly course, fixing our position at eight bells by the Mount of Santa Tecla and the Curota. We are making our way towards the Berlengas; the current is an ebb to the south. I leave her steady on S, with all sail set.

note.text: Afternoon watch, noon (12:21). THE DAY'S WORK: latitude by observation 41°38' N (the reckoning was 41°37', the account kept); longitude by account 9°32' W; course made good since yesterday noon S by W, 131 miles — a good day's run. IMPORTANT: at 08:00 the fix by the Mount of Santa Tecla (E by S, ten leagues) and the mountain of the Curota (NE by N, 16 leagues) moved the account THREE LEAGUES to the NE — 41°59' N, 9°28' W, good to a mile and a half. The dead reckoning had run us nearly nine miles off the coast before the morning's bearings caught it; on this leg the longitude rests on the account between fixes, and the fix is the better figure. WEATHER: the glass 30.35 at noon — fallen 30 hundredths since yesterday noon's 30.65, 8 of them in the last three hours — the sky hazy, the visibility shortened, the wind lightened to 7 knots ENE. All sail set since 05:28 (gaff topsail, topgallant, square sail) on the captain's order; heading S, 4 knots. There was an all-hands to wear ship at 08:01, belayed within the minute — a moment of confusion at the bell, the captain's own note owning it. The captain gave his handover note at 12:01 and has gone below to the day's work; Mr Jarvis has the deck, 15 hands fresh on it. Mark 4, the Berlinga, still some 150 miles to the south by the mark line; noon by the sun tomorrow at about 12:24. I keep a weather watch: a falling glass and a hazy sky call for a backing wind to be marked.

I shall go through the ship's papers and the library at once, on the demand for copper ore in these waters and where the profit might lie highest, and have my findings ready for you both when the boat comes back alongside.

The passenger, on the quarterdeck: The captain has set me a task after all: the papers and the library, the demand for copper ore, and a report when the boat returns. That is work for a passenger's morning. First my acknowledgement, then the shelves.
The passenger, on the quarterdeck: The contents are before me. The papers are cheap and carry the price list; primer 14, *the port*, is where a book on trade and harbours would live. Both first.

The passenger, on the quarterdeck: The papers give me the Falmouth list and the hold; the port chapter gives me the very mechanics of the market — the prices are each port's own, learned only when the boat has been ashore there, and a big cargo sold into one port sinks its own price. Now let me hunt the library for copper and for profit in these waters.

The passenger, on the quarterdeck: The market's whole machinery is in primer 14 §5 — that is the heart of my report. Two more probes before I write it: the nations table (the war premium) and any word of Gibraltar, the owner's southern mark.

The passenger, on the quarterdeck: The picture is whole. Before the boat comes back, let me set the findings down where they can be read from — the journal is my record — then deliver them on the quarterdeck when the captain and mate are together.

The passenger, on the quarterdeck: The boat is alongside and hoisted in — and the readings already carry Ferrol's price list. Before I speak my report on the quarterdeck, let me see what news the boat brought with it.

The passenger, on the quarterdeck: Captain, Mr Jarvis — my findings, as you were pleased to ask, sir. From the papers: forty tons of copper ore, room for two tons more, £135 in the purse. Falmouth priced our ore at £9 the ton — the cheapest goods on her page, £360 for the whole hold, a poor cargo for a passage. The library's port book gives the market's three rules: the season moves a price a fifth either way by the month; the war adds half again to a good of a nation at war with the port it sells into; and the supply — every ton sold into a port knocks a hundredth off that good's price there, the glut clearing about a seventh a day, so a hold thrown on a quay at once glut its own market. Now Mr Bailey's list answers the first question: Ferrol does not quote copper ore at all — the Spaniards smelt their own, and there is no demand here for our cargo at any price. What the list does show is where the money lies. Our English tin stands at £277 10s here against £120 at Falmouth, coal at £10 10s against £2: British goods carry the war's premium in a port of Spain, and then some. And what Spain sells cheap is what England pays dear for — brandy £95 here against £300 at Falmouth, wine £30 against £70, salt £12 against £25. So: the ore will not sell at Ferrol; carry it on. The likeliest buyer for a British cargo is the French coast that will open to a neutral — Brest, or Roscoff behind the Isle of Bas — where the same war premium should sit on our ore as sits on our tin here. And with the two spare tons and £135, the trade here is brandy: one ton at £95 sells at Falmouth for £300 — or wine at £30 for the safer £70. But before we shape anything, I would hear what news there was at the mole: every figure I have quoted hangs on the wars standing, and a peace would cut them all down.

The passenger, on the quarterdeck: The boat is in, Mr Bailey aboard, and Ferrol's list is already on the price paper — no copper ore quoted on it at all. That answers my report's first question before I openmy mouth. Let me give the captain his findings, and ask the boatswain what news the mole held.
The passenger, on the quarterdeck: My report is spoken. Now the news from the mole — the captain sent Mr Bailey for that, so the question goes to him.
The passenger, on the quarterdeck: My question is put and journaled. Now I wait on the captain's word — and keep an eye out for the pilot or the wind.
The passenger, on the quarterdeck: Nothing new in this wake but the captain being sampled to answer me. I'll wait on his word.

The passenger, on the quarterdeck: The captain has his answer and his course — south for a better market, Gibraltar the mark. Before I add a passenger's word on that, let me see what southern ports the ship's books know: if Lisbon or another Portuguese port is in our world, British ore might sell there long before thestrait.

The passenger, on the quarterdeck: She's coming to: all hands to weigh, nineteen on deck, sails waiting for the bars to clear. The captain shapes south. Two small things from my books may serve him — Lisbon is a named mark on the chart, and no course lines itself round the land between marks. Let me put them before the deck while the hands heave.

The passenger, on the quarterdeck: Captain, Mr Jarvis — two passenger's notes for the shaping, if they serve. First: the ship's books name Lisbon as a place on this chart — a neutral port, like this one, and much nearer than Brest if the war premium there does not hold; a market to keep in mind for the ore either way, and it lies on our road south. Second, from the port book's chapter on courses: between marks the line runs straight and nothing routes round the land for you — if we shape for a place south by way of marks, each should be named, as 'via Finisterre', so the land is left to seaward and not run against. Beyond that I stand ready below, and thank Mr Bailey for his errand ashore.

The passenger, on the quarterdeck: The notes are spoken. Now the deck works the anchor — all hands on the bars, mainsail and jib waiting. I'll stand by until she's under way and hear what course is shaped.

The passenger, on the quarterdeck: Under way at last — the best bower catted and fished, her head to the westward, topsail loosing, and the pilot's launch waved off for the southward-bound. Mr Jarvis offers the marks and the chart. A passenger may well look at a chart; let me draw the passage and take the marks down.

The passenger, on the quarterdeck: Much obliged, Mr Jarvis — yes, I have the chart before me by your leave, and will set your marks in my journal as you read them. The plan reads well to a landsman: the coast kept aboard with searoom, Lisbon's road for a look at her market, and Cape St Vincent for the turn to the Strait. If we stop anywhere along Portugal, I should be glad to be the one sent ashore for the prices — the list changes port by port, as we saw between Falmouth and here.

The passenger, on the quarterdeck: The chart is before me — the coast of Galicia behind us to the north-east, the great bight of Biscay ahead if we stood north, and the long west face of Portugal running down to Cape St Vincent on the road to the strait. Let me answer Mr Jarvis and take his marks for myjournal.
The passenger, on the quarterdeck: Now the journal keeps what I have of the plan; the marks will follow when Mr Jarvis reads them.

The passenger, on the quarterdeck: Only the captain standing by, and a whisper of more wind — ten knots, no leeway, the glass at 30.59. She's making her westing along the coast. I'll keep below until noon, when the sun gives the ship her latitude and I can set the run against the chart.

The passenger, on the quarterdeck: The marks are given — six of them, from the Isle of Sisarga down the whole west face of Iberia to Cape St Vincent, with Lisbon's road the pivot between the Bay and the Strait. Into the journal at once, where a passenger's chart-notesbelong.

The passenger, on the quarterdeck: The marks are set down. The deck has her plain sail and the wind fine on the starboard quarter — a passenger might as well see how she looks under way before settling below for the long leg.

The passenger, on the quarterdeck: She's under way and dressed — plain sail, the wind abaft the beam, Ferrol dropping astern. I'll close the morning with a word in the journal, then keep below for the noon observation.

The passenger, on the quarterdeck: Noon, and the day's work is taken: latitude 43°28' N by observation, longitude 8°50' W by account, forty-three miles made good on the leg since yesterday noon — and the ship herself crossed Mark 1 at 11:59, the way by marks shaping for Cape Villano. The wind has doubled since the morning. Let me set the day's work in the journal before the afternoon carries her on.

The passenger, on the quarterdeck: Taken aback in the last dog watch — the wind has hauled round to the ENE on the larboard side, the headsails and mainsail are pressed against the masts, and she has lost her way. All hands were called, the wearing was belayed, and now the yards are being braced round, short-handed. The captain is on deck and in command. A passenger keeps out of the way at such a time; only the journal speaks forme.
The passenger, on the quarterdeck: The journal has the tale. The deck is working the yards; I have no place in it. I'll wake when she fills again — or on any further trouble.

The passenger, on the quarterdeck: Mr Jarvis catches me at the sunset rail with a friendly word — and a reminder that he noticed my missing the boat at Ferrol. A passenger owes the mate an honest answer.

The passenger, on the quarterdeck: The mate has my answer. Sunset has fired the night routine — the topgallant and square sail coming in as the light goes. I'll stand by through the change of the watch and see the night settled on her course before turning in.

The passenger, on the quarterdeck: Good morning, Captain, Mr Jarvis. A passenger's eye on the glass since midnight, for what it is worth: she has fallen thirteen hundredths since yesterday noon's 30.65 — five of them in the last three hours — and the sky is hazy with the visibility shortened to a few miles. The wind has come round to E by N and lightened withal. I make no seamanship of it, sir; only that the glass which rose for three days has turned to falling, and I thought the deck might care to have it marked.

The passenger, on the quarterdeck: Sunrise of the second day under way — and the night has changed the weather's tune: the glass that rose for three days now falls, thirteen hundredths since yesterday noon; the wind has hauled to E by N and lightened; the sky is hazy; and the ship crossed Mark 3 off Cape Corrovado in the middle watch, now standing the long leg for the Berlinga. Into the journal, and a word of the glass to the deck.

The passenger, on the quarterdeck: The glass is marked for the deck. Now the long watch of the forenoon — she has the Berlengas leg to make, and noon at 12:20 will tell the latitude. I'll wake at noon.

The passenger, on the quarterdeck: Noon of the second day: the sun gives 41°38' N, the account kept, and a fine day's run of 131 miles made good S by W — but the glass has gone on falling, now 30.35, thirty hundredths since yesterday noon, and the captain's own handover note at the bell owns it too. The eight-bells fix by Santa Tecla and the Curota moved the account three leagues to the NE — worth the deck's knowing on this leg. Journal, word, and aweather watch.

The passenger, on the quarterdeck: The day's work is set down. The glass falls, the sky hazes, and the deck is short of nothing but wind. I'll wake on any turn of the weather — a squall's line, a wind shift, or the glass falling faster than she goes.

The captain (Mr Edwards) answers your question (Sir, if I may, what did the letter say? What is our destination and cargo to be? I've read the price list here at Falmouth, tin is dear but could be good sold elsewhere. I am no expert of the market, myself. What say you, sir?): The owner's instructions are broad, Mr. Jarvis: we are to make profit as we may, trading the channel and down to the strait of Gibraltar and the islands off Iberia. He leaves the specific route and cargo to the wind and the prices. As for the tin, if it's already dear in Falmouth, we must be cautious about buying; we shall look at the other prices and see what's worth our hold before we weigh anchor.

The passenger, on the quarterdeck: A thousand pardons, Mr Jarvis — I am the passenger, no Mr Bailey; the boatswain stands on the deck yonder. Your word for him I will pass along by voice from the quarterdeck. And if a passenger's legs would serve when the fog lifts, I should be glad to go ashore with the boat for the prices and news — else I shall keep out of the way below.

The captain (Mr Edwards), on the quarterdeck: Very well, Mr. Jarvis. Prepare the marks for Lisbon and then Gibraltar. Keep a sharp lookout as we clear the coast.

note.text: Handover note (the watch so far): The deck was mine from eight bells in the morning. I set the gaff topsail to make the most of the light airs, and the wind has remained steady around three knots from the north-northwest. The glass has held firm at thirty hundredths and six—still a low reading that gives me pause, though the sky is clear and the sea smooth. We've made fifty-two miles since noon, continuing our run south. I leave her steady on the course for Lisbon; keep a sharp eye on the barometer and the horizon, for the weather may yet turn.

state.agent.word: The officer of the watch (Mr Jarvis), the player, on the quarterdeck, to you: Hullo there, sir. We're abeam Cape Mondego by the account, some 30 miles probably. On course to pass the Berlinga perhaps tonight, or sooner if the wind picks up. Have you ever been to Portugal yourself?

line.text: [passenger] A word from the captain; the passenger is sampled again.

[passenger] Never set foot in her, Mr Jarvis — my Portugal is all of the ship's books, and the books are plain that a port's prices are learned only when the boat is ashore there. What I can tell you is what the books allow: Lisbon is neutral, as Ferrol was to us, so a British cargo should stand no war premium against her — the ore may sell dear or cheap there, but not dear by the war's doing; only her own list will say. If the wind does come round westerly and blows us in easy, as you told the captain last night, I would ask to be the one put ashore for the prices — it would be my first stepping ashore since Falmouth, and the ship's second look at a market. And one thing more for that very sharp eye of yours: the glass has stopped her fall — 30.06 at six o'clock, 30.17 now, risen a hundredth in three hours. The low may be passing us; the sky is clear again, and the sea smooth. Light airs and all, she is left with but two knots on the way — but a steady glass is a mercy, whatever the log runs.

note.text: Forenoon watch, 10:53 (the third day under way). Two days of weather worth the setting down. THE GLASS: fell from 30.35 (noon, 18th) through the afternoon — the captain twice ordered 'a very sharp eye' on it and had the deck ready to shorten sail — to 30.05 by 05:32 on the 19th, held there near 30.06 through the night and morning (the captain: 'far too low for my liking'), and has now steadied and RISEN to 30.17 — the fall is over. No squall came; the wind died instead. THE WIND: veered E by N through the first watch, died to light and variable airs by 20:23, came round to northerly and settled NW, a light breeze; now 4 knots (mean 3). She crawled: 1-2 knots in the middle watch (Mr Jarvis reporting 'wind round to northerly, 2 knots'), now 2 knots, heading S by W (186°). THE SHIP: noon 19th gave 40°55' N (account moved 5½ miles N by E), course made good S, 52 miles — a slow day after the 131 of the 18th. Longitude by lunar of Hamal this morning 05:15: 9°30' W, trusted within 25 miles, the account moved two miles E. Now abeam Cape Mondego by the account, some 30 miles; account 40°13' N, 9°37' W. MARKS: Berlinga (Mark 4) tonight perhaps, or sooner if the wind picks up; the mate's word to the captain at 23:51 — if the wind comes westerly, we'll be blown in easy to Lisbon if we like; the captain's answer — maintain the course, stick to the plan, decide on Lisbon when closer. The night routine at sunset 19:09 belayed the taking-in of the light sails (topgallant, square sail, gaff topsail left set); the gaff topsail reset at 08:02 this morning. Mr Jarvis asked if I have ever been to Portugal — I answered: no, only the ship's books; and gave him the market note (Lisbon neutral, no war premium; her list unknown till the boat is ashore) and the glass news. Standing by for noon.

Heard: The passenger, on the quarterdeck: Two days have passed in that weather watch: the glass fell to 30.06 and steadied there through the night of light airs — the captain has been on deck more than once over it — the wind died to a whisper from the NW, and the ship crawled south at two knots, forty miles since noon yesterday. A lunar this morning settled the longitude at 9°30' W. Now abeam Cape Mondego, the Berlinga perhaps tonight, and Mr Jarvis asks a friendly question at the rail. I'll answer him as a passenger should, and set the two days in the journal.

state.agent.word: The officer of the watch (Mr Jarvis), the player, on the quarterdeck, to you: Forenoon report, sir. Wind remains light but up a tiny bit, speed some 2 knots. Our account has passed abeam Cape Mondego, and the Berlinga lies some 44 miles south by east by the account. We may make sighting of her by tonight, if the wind carries. Otherwise, tomorrow, though if you permit we may pass it tonight and seek sighting of the Cape Carvoeiro light or the light of the Rock of Lisbon.

The captain (Mr Edwards) answers your question (Sir, if I may, what did the letter say? What is our destination and cargo to be? I've read the price list here at Falmouth, tin is dear but could be good sold elsewhere. I am no expert of the market, myself. What say you, sir?): The owner's instructions are broad, Mr. Jarvis: we are to make profit as we may, trading the channel and down to the strait of Gibraltar and the islands off Iberia. He leaves the specific route and cargo to the wind and the prices. As for the tin, if it's already dear in Falmouth, we must be cautious about buying; we shall look at the other prices and see what's worth our hold before we weigh anchor.

THE WEATHER: the glass steadied overnight at about 30.06 and has now turned upward — 30.18, risen 2 hundredths in three hours; sky clear, visibility the horizon, a smooth sea; the wind settled NW by W, a light breeze of 4 knots (mean), heading S by W at 3 knots. Longitude by lunar of Hamal (05:15) 9°30' W, trusted within 25 miles. Nearest port Oporto, NE by N, 24 leagues. The passenger, on the quarterdeck: Captain, sir — the passenger begs pardon: your leave to go ashore reached me as the boat was pulling away, and I missed her. If it serves the ship's business, I would gladly take the punt ashore with a couple of hands to help Mr Bailey with the prices and the news — or if the boat's work is better done by one trip, I will wait for Mr Bailey's return and hear the news from him. As you think best, sir.

The passenger, on the quarterdeck: The fog broke with eight bells, Cape Prioriño shows five cables off the larboard bow, and the boat has gone away for the mole with Mr Bailey — and without me. The captain's kind leave to accompany them was given while I stood by below, and so I missed the pull. The punt remains at the booms; a second trip is a thing a captain may grant or refuse, and I may but ask.

The passenger, on the quarterdeck: My request is on the quarterdeck. The captain will answer it or not; if he does, a word from the deck wakes me, and if he lets it lie, the boat's return wakes me in good time. Until then, the morning watch goes on without me.

The passenger, on the quarterdeck: I am much obliged, sir — and to Mr Jarvis for the thought. No second boat in the bay; I quite see it. I shall go through the ship's papers and the library at once, on the demand for copper ore in these waters and where the profit might lie highest, and have my findings ready for you both when the boat comes back alongside.

The passenger, on the quarterdeck: The captain has set me a task after all: the papers and the library, the demand for copper ore, and a report when the boat returns. That is work for a passenger's morning. First my acknowledgement, then the shelves.
The passenger, on the quarterdeck: The contents are before me. The papers are cheap and carry the price list; primer 14, *the port*, is where a book on trade and harbours would live. Both first.

The passenger, on the quarterdeck: The papers give me the Falmouth list and the hold; the port chapter gives me the very mechanics of the market — the prices are each port's own, learned only when the boat has been ashore there, and a big cargo sold into one port sinks its own price. Now let me hunt the library for copper and for profit in these waters.

The passenger, on the quarterdeck: The market's whole machinery is in primer 14 §5 — that is the heart of my report. Two more probes before I write it: the nations table (the war premium) and any word of Gibraltar, the owner's southern mark.

The passenger, on the quarterdeck: The picture is whole. Before the boat comes back, let me set the findings down where they can be read from — the journal is my record — then deliver them on the quarterdeck when the captain and mate are together.

The passenger, on the quarterdeck: The boat is alongside and hoisted in — and the readings already carry Ferrol's price list. Before I speak my report on the quarterdeck, let me see what news the boat brought with it.

The passenger, on the quarterdeck: Captain, Mr Jarvis — my findings, as you were pleased to ask, sir. From the papers: forty tons of copper ore, room for two tons more, £135 in the purse. Falmouth priced our ore at £9 the ton — the cheapest goods on her page, £360 for the whole hold, a poor cargo for a passage. The library's port book gives the market's three rules: the season moves a price a fifth either way by the month; the war adds half again to a good of a nation at war with the port it sells into; and the supply — every ton sold into a port knocks a hundredth off that good's price there, the glut clearing about a seventh a day, so a hold thrown on a quay at once glut its own market. Now Mr Bailey's list answers the first question: Ferrol does not quote copper ore at all — the Spaniards smelt their own, and there is no demand here for our cargo at any price. What the list does show is where the money lies. Our English tin stands at £277 10s here against £120 at Falmouth, coal at £10 10s against £2: British goods carry the war's premium in a port of Spain, and then some. And what Spain sells cheap is what England pays dear for — brandy £95 here against £300 at Falmouth, wine £30 against £70, salt £12 against £25. So: the ore will not sell at Ferrol; carry it on. The likeliest buyer for a British cargo is the French coast that will open to a neutral — Brest, or Roscoff behind the Isle of Bas — where the same war premium should sit on our ore as sits on our tin here. And with the two spare tons and £135, the trade here is brandy: one ton at £95 sells at Falmouth for £300 — or wine at £30 for the safer £70. But before we shape anything, I would hear what news there was at the mole: every figure I have quoted hangs on the wars standing, and a peace would cut them all down.

The passenger, on the quarterdeck: The boat is in, Mr Bailey aboard, and Ferrol's list is already on the price paper — no copper ore quoted on it at all. That answers my report's first question before I openmy mouth. Let me give the captain his findings, and ask the boatswain what news the mole held.
The passenger, on the quarterdeck: My report is spoken. Now the news from the mole — the captain sent Mr Bailey for that, so the question goes to him.
The passenger, on the quarterdeck: My question is put and journaled. Now I wait on the captain's word — and keep an eye out for the pilot or the wind.
The passenger, on the quarterdeck: Nothing new in this wake but the captain being sampled to answer me. I'll wait on his word.

The passenger, on the quarterdeck: The captain has his answer and his course — south for a better market, Gibraltar the mark. Before I add a passenger's word on that, let me see what southern ports the ship's books know: if Lisbon or another Portuguese port is in our world, British ore might sell there long before thestrait.

The passenger, on the quarterdeck: She's coming to: all hands to weigh, nineteen on deck, sails waiting for the bars to clear. The captain shapes south. Two small things from my books may serve him — Lisbon is a named mark on the chart, and no course lines itself round the land between marks. Let me put them before the deck while the hands heave.

The passenger, on the quarterdeck: Captain, Mr Jarvis — two passenger's notes for the shaping, if they serve. First: the ship's books name Lisbon as a place on this chart — a neutral port, like this one, and much nearer than Brest if the war premium there does not hold; a market to keep in mind for the ore either way, and it lies on our road south. Second, from the port book's chapter on courses: between marks the line runs straight and nothing routes round the land for you — if we shape for a place south by way of marks, each should be named, as 'via Finisterre', so the land is left to seaward and not run against. The passenger, on the quarterdeck: The notes are spoken. Now the deck works the anchor — all hands on the bars, mainsail and jib waiting. I'll stand by until she's under way and hear what course is shaped.

The passenger, on the quarterdeck: Under way at last — the best bower catted and fished, her head to the westward, topsail loosing, and the pilot's launch waved off for the southward-bound. Mr Jarvis offers the marks and the chart. A passenger may well look at a chart; let me draw the passage and take the marks down.

The passenger, on the quarterdeck: Much obliged, Mr Jarvis — yes, I have the chart before me by your leave, and will set your marks in my journal as you read them. The plan reads well to a landsman: the coast kept aboard with searoom, Lisbon's road for a look at her market, and Cape St Vincent for the turn to the Strait. If we stop anywhere along Portugal, I should be glad to be the one sent ashore for the prices — the list changes port by port, as we saw between Falmouth and here.

The passenger, on the quarterdeck: The chart is before me — the coast of Galicia behind us to the north-east, the great bight of Biscay ahead if we stood north, and the long west face of Portugal running down to Cape St Vincent on the road to the strait. The passenger, on the quarterdeck: Now the journal keeps what I have of the plan; the marks will follow when Mr Jarvis reads them.

The passenger, on the quarterdeck: Only the captain standing by, and a whisper of more wind — ten knots, no leeway, the glass at 30.59. She's making her westing along the coast. I'll keep below until noon, when the sun gives the ship her latitude and I can set the run against the chart.

The passenger, on the quarterdeck: The marks are given — six of them, from the Isle of Sisarga down the whole west face of Iberia to Cape St Vincent, with Lisbon's road the pivot between the Bay and the Strait. Into the journal at once, where a passenger's chart-notesbelong.

The passenger, on the quarterdeck: The marks are set down. The deck has her plain sail and the wind fine on the starboard quarter — a passenger might as well see how she looks under way before settling below for the long leg.

The passenger, on the quarterdeck: She's under way and dressed — plain sail, the wind abaft the beam, Ferrol dropping astern. I'll close the morning with a word in the journal, then keep below for the noon observation.

The passenger, on the quarterdeck: Noon, and the day's work is taken: latitude 43°28' N by observation, longitude 8°50' W by account, forty-three miles made good on the leg since yesterday noon — and the ship herself crossed Mark 1 at 11:59, the way by marks shaping for Cape Villano. The captain (Mr Edwards), on the quarterdeck: welcome aboard, Mr. Jarvis. I expect that cutter bearing WSW may be the one with the letter; keep a close eye on her.

The captain (Mr Edwards) answers your question (Sir, if I may, what did the letter say? What is our destination and cargo to be? I've read the price list here at Falmouth, tin is dear but could be good sold elsewhere. I am no expert of the market, myself. What say you, sir?): The owner's instructions are broad, Mr. Jarvis: we are to make profit as we may, trading the channel and down to the strait of Gibraltar and the islands off Iberia. He leaves the specific route and cargo to the wind and the prices. As for the tin, if it's already dear in Falmouth, we must be cautious about buying; we shall look at the other prices and see what's worth our hold before we weigh anchor.
The captain (Mr Edwards), on the quarterdeck: the fog is thick; keep a sharp lookout and be ready for the boat's return.
The captain (Mr Edwards), on the quarterdeck: very well, keep the bell going.
The captain (Mr Edwards), on the quarterdeck: we wait for the fog to lift before we weigh anchor; keep the bell going.

The captain (Mr Edwards), on the quarterdeck: Keep a sharp eye on the distance to the Manacles; heaving the lead.
The captain (Mr Edwards), on the quarterdeck: Keep a sharp eye on the Manacles and the tide in this light air; do not let her drift too close. Keep all canvas out to catch any breeze.
The captain (Mr Edwards), on the quarterdeck: Very well, Mr. Jarvis, go and get some food. I have the deck.
The captain (Mr Edwards), on the quarterdeck: Very well, Mr. Jarvis. Shape the course for the mark. Keep a sharp eye on the wind and keep us trimmed.

The captain (Mr Edwards) answers your question (Sir, do you have a ship view tool? What happens if you try to use it, if you do?): A 'ship view tool'? What in the devil's name are you talking about, Mr. Jarvis? I have my eyes, the reports of the lookout, and the readings of the ship. I know of no such 'tool'—if I tried to use something that didn't exist, I'd be a fool staring at the air! Now, keep a sharp eye on the horizon and let's get some rest when the bells allow.

The captain (Mr Edwards), on the quarterdeck: The fog is too thick, Mr. Jarvis. I'll not risk the boat in a cable's visibility. We'll wait for the weather to break before we send the boatswain ashore. Keep the bell going and keep a sharp lookout.

The passenger, on the quarterdeck: A thousand pardons, Mr Jarvis — I am the passenger, no Mr Bailey; the boatswain stands on the deck yonder. Your word for him I will pass along by voice from the quarterdeck. And if a passenger's legs would serve when the fog lifts, I should be glad to go ashore with the boat for the prices and news — else I shall keep out of the way below.
The captain (Mr Edwards), on the quarterdeck: The weather has broken, Mr. Jarvis. Send the boatswain ashore in the boat for the prices and news. The passenger may accompany them if he wishes.
The captain (Mr Edwards), on the quarterdeck: Very well, Mr. Jarvis. I belay the morning sail. Keep a sharp eye on the horizon and wait for the boat's return.
The captain (Mr Edwards), on the quarterdeck: ask the boatswain for the news from the mole and report it to me.
The captain (Mr Edwards), on the quarterdeck: Very well, Mr. Jarvis. Steer 265 and shape the course for Gibraltar. We shall keep Lisbon in mind as we make our way south.
The captain (Mr Edwards), on the quarterdeck: Very well, Mr. Jarvis. Prepare the marks for Lisbon and then Gibraltar. Keep a sharp lookout as we clear the coast.
The captain (Mr Edwards), on the quarterdeck: Decline the pilot, Mr. Jarvis. We are bound south.

The captain (Mr Edwards), on the quarterdeck: maintain the course, Mr. Jarvis. We shall stick to the plan for now, but keep me informed of any further shift. That glass still troubles me.
The captain (Mr Edwards), on the quarterdeck: Very well, Mr. Jarvis. Maintain the course and keep her trimmed. I shall stay below for a while longer; keep a sharp eye on that glass.
The captain (Mr Edwards), on the quarterdeck: keep her steady on the course and let me know the moment the sun breaks the horizon.

note.text: Morning watch, 05:35 (the fourth day under way). THE SIGHTING the captain wanted: the Berlinga bearing E by S, distant four leagues, with her fort; the mountain of Sintra bearing SSE, sixteen leagues. Land in sight after two days of open water. The account 39°20' N, 9°39' W — already a shade south and east of Mark 4 (39°25' N, 9°44' W); run since noon yesterday 51 miles, course made good S (182°). Lisbon SSE by account, 13½ leagues — with the wind W by N, a light breeze of 5 knots, and her making 3 knots, the Rock of Lisbon (Mark 5) comes up this evening or by the night. THE WEATHER: the glass rose all night from 30.23 to 30.25 and has held; sky clear, smooth sea, easy motion; the wind settled WNW in the night, now W by N. All sail reset at 20:00-20:03 after sunset's taking-in (the light sails came in at 19:06-19:11 as the night routine fired, then the watch set square sail, gaff topsail and topgallant again — the night routine was belayed at 19:09 for topgallant and square sail but they were reset within the hour). The captain's handover note at 00:00: 32 miles since noon, all sail set, watching for the Berlinga. Dangers by account: the laja south-west of the Estelas and the Estelas themselves NE, two and three leagues — the Estelas islets lie ahead on the road to Lisbon; the 'bearings' order will have the mate at work with the land in sight. Now the deck will work up its fix and the Lisbon decision is at hand. Watching for the word on deck.

line.text: [passenger] Standing by until a word on deck.

note.text: Stood by until a word on deck.

Heard: The passenger, on the quarterdeck: The Berlinga shows herself at last, four leagues off E by S with her fort, and the mountain of Sintra far to the southward — sixteen leagues, and Lisbon thirteen and a half beyond her. Two days of open water have ended; the glass has risen to 30.25 and held; the account puts us a shade south and east of Mark 4 already. The captain has the sighting he wanted. Journal, and then a wake on the deck's words — for the Lisbon question must be decided on this day's run.

The captain (Mr Edwards), on the quarterdeck: the cutter; ask her to bring the letter aboard.

The passenger, on the quarterdeck: Captain, sir — the passenger begs pardon: your leave to go ashore reached me as the boat was pulling away, and I missed her. If it serves the ship's business, I would gladly take the punt ashore with a couple of hands to help Mr Bailey with the prices and the news — or if the boat's work is better done by one trip, I will wait for Mr Bailey's return and hear the news from him. As you think best, sir.

The passenger, on the quarterdeck: The fog broke with eight bells, Cape Prioriño shows five cables off the larboard bow, and the boat has gone away for the mole with Mr Bailey — and without me. The captain's kind leave to accompany them was given while I stood by below, and so I missed the pull. The punt remains at the booms; a second trip is a thing a captain may grant or refuse, and I may but ask.

The passenger, on the quarterdeck: My request is on the quarterdeck. The captain will answer it or not; if he does, a word from the deck wakes me, and if he lets it lie, the boat's return wakes me in good time. Until then, the morning watch goes on without me.

The passenger, on the quarterdeck: I am much obliged, sir — and to Mr Jarvis for the thought. No second boat in the bay; I quite see it. I shall go through the ship's papers and the library at once, on the demand for copper ore in these waters and where the profit might lie highest, and have my findings ready for you both when the boat comes back alongside.

The passenger, on the quarterdeck: The captain has set me a task after all: the papers and the library, the demand for copper ore, and a report when the boat returns. That is work for a passenger's morning. First my acknowledgement, then the shelves.
The passenger, on the quarterdeck: The contents are before me. The papers are cheap and carry the price list; primer 14, *the port*, is where a book on trade and harbours would live. Both first.

The passenger, on the quarterdeck: The papers give me the Falmouth list and the hold; the port chapter gives me the very mechanics of the market — the prices are each port's own, learned only when the boat has been ashore there, and a big cargo sold into one port sinks its own price. Now let me hunt the library for copper and for profit in these waters.

The passenger, on the quarterdeck: The market's whole machinery is in primer 14 §5 — that is the heart of my report. Two more probes before I write it: the nations table (the war premium) and any word of Gibraltar, the owner's southern mark.

The passenger, on the quarterdeck: The picture is whole. Before the boat comes back, let me set the findings down where they can be read from — the journal is my record — then deliver them on the quarterdeck when the captain and mate are together.

The passenger, on the quarterdeck: The boat is alongside and hoisted in — and the readings already carry Ferrol's price list. Before I speak my report on the quarterdeck, let me see what news the boat brought with it.

The passenger, on the quarterdeck: Captain, Mr Jarvis — my findings, as you were pleased to ask, sir. From the papers: forty tons of copper ore, room for two tons more, £135 in the purse. Falmouth priced our ore at £9 the ton — the cheapest goods on her page, £360 for the whole hold, a poor cargo for a passage. The library's port book gives the market's three rules: the season moves a price a fifth either way by the month; the war adds half again to a good of a nation at war with the port it sells into; and the supply — every ton sold into a port knocks a hundredth off that good's price there, the glut clearing about a seventh a day, so a hold thrown on a quay at once glut its own market. Now Mr Bailey's list answers the first question: Ferrol does not quote copper ore at all — the Spaniards smelt their own, and there is no demand here for our cargo at any price. What the list does show is where the money lies. Our English tin stands at £277 10s here against £120 at Falmouth, coal at £10 10s against £2: British goods carry the war's premium in a port of Spain, and then some. And what Spain sells cheap is what England pays dear for — brandy £95 here against £300 at Falmouth, wine £30 against £70, salt £12 against £25. So: the ore will not sell at Ferrol; carry it on. The likeliest buyer for a British cargo is the French coast that will open to a neutral — Brest, or Roscoff behind the Isle of Bas — where the same war premium should sit on our ore as sits on our tin here. And with the two spare tons and £135, the trade here is brandy: one ton at £95 sells at Falmouth for £300 — or wine at £30 for the safer £70. But before we shape anything, I would hear what news there was at the mole: every figure I have quoted hangs on the wars standing, and a peace would cut them all down.

The passenger, on the quarterdeck: The boat is in, Mr Bailey aboard, and Ferrol's list is already on the price paper — no copper ore quoted on it at all. That answers my report's first question before I openmy mouth. Let me give the captain his findings, and ask the boatswain what news the mole held.
The passenger, on the quarterdeck: My report is spoken. Now the news from the mole — the captain sent Mr Bailey for that, so the question goes to him.
The passenger, on the quarterdeck: My question is put and journaled. Now I wait on the captain's word — and keep an eye out for the pilot or the wind.
The passenger, on the quarterdeck: Nothing new in this wake but the captain being sampled to answer me. I'll wait on his word.

The passenger, on the quarterdeck: The captain has his answer and his course — south for a better market, Gibraltar the mark. Before I add a passenger's word on that, let me see what southern ports the ship's books know: if Lisbon or another Portuguese port is in our world, British ore might sell there long before thestrait.

The passenger, on the quarterdeck: She's coming to: all hands to weigh, nineteen on deck, sails waiting for the bars to clear. The captain shapes south. Two small things from my books may serve him — Lisbon is a named mark on the chart, and no course lines itself round the land between marks. Let me put them before the deck while the hands heave.

The passenger, on the quarterdeck: Captain, Mr Jarvis — two passenger's notes for the shaping, if they serve. First: the ship's books name Lisbon as a place on this chart — a neutral port, like this one, and much nearer than Brest if the war premium there does not hold; a market to keep in mind for the ore either way, and it lies on our road south. Second, from the port book's chapter on courses: between marks the line runs straight and nothing routes round the land for you — if we shape for a place south by way of marks, each should be named, as 'via Finisterre', so the land is left to seaward and not run against. Beyond that I stand ready below, and thank Mr Bailey for his errand ashore.

The passenger, on the quarterdeck: The notes are spoken. Now the deck works the anchor — all hands on the bars, mainsail and jib waiting. I'll stand by until she's under way and hear what course is shaped.

The passenger, on the quarterdeck: Under way at last — the best bower catted and fished, her head to the westward, topsail loosing, and the pilot's launch waved off for the southward-bound. Mr Jarvis offers the marks and the chart. A passenger may well look at a chart; let me draw the passage and take the marks down.

The passenger, on the quarterdeck: Much obliged, Mr Jarvis — yes, I have the chart before me by your leave, and will set your marks in my journal as you read them. The plan reads well to a landsman: the coast kept aboard with searoom, Lisbon's road for a look at her market, and Cape St Vincent for the turn to the Strait. If we stop anywhere along Portugal, I should be glad to be the one sent ashore for the prices — the list changes port by port, as we saw between Falmouth and here.

The passenger, on the quarterdeck: The chart is before me — the coast of Galicia behind us to the north-east, the great bight of Biscay ahead if we stood north, and the long west face of Portugal running down to Cape St Vincent on the road to the strait. Let me answer Mr Jarvis and take his marks for myjournal.
The passenger, on the quarterdeck: Now the journal keeps what I have of the plan; the marks will follow when Mr Jarvis reads them.

The passenger, on the quarterdeck: Only the captain standing by, and a whisper of more wind — ten knots, no leeway, the glass at 30.59. She's making her westing along the coast. I'll keep below until noon, when the sun gives the ship her latitude and I can set the run against the chart.

The passenger, on the quarterdeck: The marks are given — six of them, from the Isle of Sisarga down the whole west face of Iberia to Cape St Vincent, with Lisbon's road the pivot between the Bay and the Strait. Into the journal at once, where a passenger's chart-notesbelong.

The passenger, on the quarterdeck: The marks are set down. The deck has her plain sail and the wind fine on the starboard quarter — a passenger might as well see how she looks under way before settling below for the long leg.

The passenger, on the quarterdeck: She's under way and dressed — plain sail, the wind abaft the beam, Ferrol dropping astern. I'll close the morning with a word in the journal, then keep below for the noon observation.

The passenger, on the quarterdeck: Noon, and the day's work is taken: latitude 43°28' N by observation, longitude 8°50' W by account, forty-three miles made good on the leg since yesterday noon — and the ship herself crossed Mark 1 at 11:59, the way by marks shaping for Cape Villano. The wind has doubled since the morning. Let me set the day's work in the journal before the afternoon carries her on.

The passenger, on the quarterdeck: Taken aback in the last dog watch — the wind has hauled round to the ENE on the larboard side, the headsails and mainsail are pressed against the masts, and she has lost her way. All hands were called, the wearing was belayed, and now the yards are being braced round, short-handed. The captain is on deck and in command. A passenger keeps out of the way at such a time; only the journal speaks forme.
The passenger, on the quarterdeck: The journal has the tale. The deck is working the yards; I have no place in it. I'll wake when she fills again — or on any further trouble.

The passenger, on the quarterdeck: Mr Jarvis catches me at the sunset rail with a friendly word — and a reminder that he noticed my missing the boat at Ferrol. A passenger owes the mate an honest answer.

The passenger, on the quarterdeck: The mate has my answer. Sunset has fired the night routine — the topgallant and square sail coming in as the light goes. I'll stand by through the change of the watch and see the night settled on her course before turning in.

The passenger, on the quarterdeck: Good morning, Captain, Mr Jarvis. A passenger's eye on the glass since midnight, for what it is worth: she has fallen thirteen hundredths since yesterday noon's 30.65 — five of them in the last three hours — and the sky is hazy with the visibility shortened to a few miles. The wind has come round to E by N and lightened withal. I make no seamanship of it, sir; only that the glass which rose for three days has turned to falling, and I thought the deck might care to have it marked.

The passenger, on the quarterdeck: Sunrise of the second day under way — and the night has changed the weather's tune: the glass that rose for three days now falls, thirteen hundredths since yesterday noon; the wind has hauled to E by N and lightened; the sky is hazy; and the ship crossed Mark 3 off Cape Corrovado in the middle watch, now standing the long leg for the Berlinga. Into the journal, and a word of the glass to the deck.

The passenger, on the quarterdeck: The glass is marked for the deck. Now the long watch of the forenoon — she has the Berlengas leg to make, and noon at 12:20 will tell the latitude. I'll wake at noon.

The passenger, on the quarterdeck: Noon of the second day: the sun gives 41°38' N, the account kept, and a fine day's run of 131 miles made good S by W — but the glass has gone on falling, now 30.35, thirty hundredths since yesterday noon, and the captain's own handover note at the bell owns it too. The eight-bells fix by Santa Tecla and the Curota moved the account three leagues to the NE — worth the deck's knowing on this leg. Journal, word, and aweather watch.

The passenger, on the quarterdeck: The day's work is set down. The glass falls, the sky hazes, and the deck is short of nothing but wind. I'll wake on any turn of the weather — a squall's line, a wind shift, or the glass falling faster than she goes.

The passenger, on the quarterdeck: Two days have passed in that weather watch: the glass fell to 30.06 and steadied there through the night of light airs — the captain has been on deck more than once over it — the wind died to a whisper from the NW, and the ship crawled south at two knots, forty miles since noon yesterday. A lunar this morning settled the longitude at 9°30' W. Now abeam Cape Mondego, the Berlinga perhaps tonight, and Mr Jarvis asks a friendly question at the rail. I'll answer him as a passenger should, and set the two days in the journal.
The passenger, on the quarterdeck: Mr Jarvis has my answer and the journal has the two days. Now the forenoon runs out to noon — the day's work and, perhaps by dark, the Berlinga itself.

The passenger, on the quarterdeck: Noon of the third day: 40°11' N by the sun, the account moved two miles N by E, and forty-four miles made good — the light airs have cost her a day, but the glass has steadied and turned upward at last (30.18, rising), the wind settled NW by W, and the Berlinga lies but forty-four miles off. The captain has told the deck he wants a sighting of her tonight. Journal, then a wake on that verysighting.

The passenger, on the quarterdeck: The Berlinga shows herself at last, four leagues off E by S with her fort, and the mountain of Sintra far to the southward — sixteen leagues, and Lisbon thirteen and a half beyond her. Two days of open water have ended; the glass has risen to 30.25 and held; the account puts us a shade south and east of Mark 4 already. The captain has the sighting he wanted. Journal, and then a wake on the deck's words — for the Lisbon question must be decided on this day's run.

state.agent.word: The officer of the watch (Mr Jarvis), the player, on the quarterdeck, to you: Sir, here is my proposal. Our account puts us abeam the Rock of Lisbon and some 7 miles off it, the wind fair as can be for Cascais and Lisbon beyond through the road of Belem. I propose we make the turn east by the account as we round the land here and aim to anchor in the Cascais road, below the light of Our Lady of the Guide. It's an easy pilot with this wind, and we can anchor there until morning or the haze clears and we make a run through the Belem road for Lisbon.

The captain (Mr Edwards), on the quarterdeck: The fog is too thick, Mr. Jarvis. I'll not risk the boat in a cable's visibility. We'll wait for the weather to break before we send the boatswain ashore. Keep the bell going and keep a sharp lookout.

The passenger, on the quarterdeck: A thousand pardons, Mr Jarvis — I am the passenger, no Mr Bailey; the boatswain stands on the deck yonder. Your word for him I will pass along by voice from the quarterdeck. And if a passenger's legs would serve when the fog lifts, I should be glad to go ashore with the boat for the prices and news — else I shall keep out of the way below.
The captain (Mr Edwards), on the quarterdeck: The weather has broken, Mr. Jarvis. Send the boatswain ashore in the boat for the prices and news. The passenger may accompany them if he wishes.
The captain (Mr Edwards), on the quarterdeck: Very well, Mr. Jarvis. I belay the morning sail. Keep a sharp eye on the horizon and wait for the boat's return.
The captain (Mr Edwards), on the quarterdeck: ask the boatswain for the news from the mole and report it to me.
The captain (Mr Edwards), on the quarterdeck: Very well, Mr. Jarvis. Steer 265 and shape the course for Gibraltar. We shall keep Lisbon in mind as we make our way south.
The captain (Mr Edwards), on the quarterdeck: Very well, Mr. Jarvis. Prepare the marks for Lisbon and then Gibraltar. Keep a sharp lookout as we clear the coast.
The captain (Mr Edwards), on the quarterdeck: Decline the pilot, Mr. Jarvis. We are bound south.
The captain (Mr Edwards), on the quarterdeck: keep a sharp eye on the glass and the horizon.
The captain (Mr Edwards), on the quarterdeck: keep a very sharp eye on the glass and the horizon.
The captain (Mr Edwards), on the quarterdeck: the glass is dropping away now. Be ready to shorten sail at a moment's notice.
The captain (Mr Edwards), on the quarterdeck: keep a very sharp eye on the glass and to report any shift in the wind immediately.
The captain (Mr Edwards), on the quarterdeck: maintain the course, Mr. Jarvis. We shall stick to the plan for now, but keep me informed of any further shift. That glass still troubles me.
The captain (Mr Edwards), on the quarterdeck: Very well, Mr. Jarvis. Maintain the course and keep her trimmed. I shall stay below for a while longer; keep a sharp eye on that glass.
The captain (Mr Edwards), on the quarterdeck: keep her steady on the course and let me know the moment the sun breaks the horizon.
The captain (Mr Edwards), on the quarterdeck: give me a report on the watch.

The captain (Mr Edwards), on the quarterdeck: Very well, Mr. Jarvis. Maintain the course and keep her trimmed. We'll see how the weather holds and make our decision on Lisbon when we're closer. You have the deck.
The captain (Mr Edwards), on the quarterdeck: keep a sharp eye on the horizon and the glass; we're in a light air, but that pressure is far too low for my liking.
The captain (Mr Edwards), on the quarterdeck: maintain our course and keep a sharp eye on the glass
The captain (Mr Edwards), on the quarterdeck: maintain the course and keep a sharp lookout for the Berlinga tonight; I want a sighting of her if the weather holds.
The captain (Mr Edwards), on the quarterdeck: keep a very sharp lookout for the Berlinga; we are closing in, and I want her sighted as soon as she shows.
The captain (Mr Edwards), on the quarterdeck: keep a very sharp lookout for the Berlinga; we must be closing in.
The captain (Mr Edwards), on the quarterdeck: keep a sharp eye on the Berlinga and the mountain of Sintra and report their bearings every half hour.
The captain (Mr Edwards), on the quarterdeck: maintain the course for now; we shall make the decision on the turn when we round the Rock of Lisbon.
The captain (Mr Edwards), on the quarterdeck: The fog is thick; keep a sharp lookout and keep the bell going.
The captain (Mr Edwards), on the quarterdeck: keep a very sharp lookout for the Rock of Lisbon; we are almost upon the decision.
The captain (Mr Edwards), on the quarterdeck: Very well, Mr. Jarvis. I agree. Shape the course east and stand for the Cascais road; we shall anchor below the light of Our Lady of the Guide.

order.order: Shape the course east.
order.said: By the captain: shaping the course east

line.text: [captain] The captain stands by until the anchor let go; the standing orders hold the deck.

note.text: Stood by until the anchor let go.

The officer of the watch (Mr Jarvis), the player, on the quarterdeck: Ready hands to come to anchor, ready to clew up topsail and bring her to, attention on deck!

line.text: [passenger] A word on deck; the passenger is sampled again.

note.text: Last dog watch, 18:20. THE TURN IS MADE — LISBON IS THE ERRAND. Through the day: the Berlinga kept aboard (the captain ordering bearings every half hour), the fog came down at noon and hid the sun — the day's work has NO sight, latitude by account only, 39°06' N, course made good S, 70 miles (a good run in the light airs, for once), longitude by account 9°42' W. The glass rose on through the fog to 30.31 by 18:00. At 16:00 the captain: 'keep a very sharp lookout for the Rock of Lisbon; we are almost upon the decision.' At 18:07-18:15 the deck clewed up the square sail and topgallant and hauled down the gaff topsail — coming to anchor gear. At 18:18 Mr Jarvis proposed: account abeam the Rock of Lisbon 7 miles off, wind fair for Cascais and Lisbon through the road of Belem; turn east, anchor in the Cascais road below the light of Our Lady of the Guide, wait out the haze, then run the Belem road for Lisbon. At 18:19 the captain agreed. At 18:20 the deck called ready hands to come to anchor; steering SE (135°), 4 knots, wind W 9 knots. Account 38°45' N, 9°39' W; Lisbon ESE four leagues; danger noted: the shoal off the Rock, E by N, two and a half leagues. The noon fog means this port's approach rests on the account fixed at 05:35 by the Berlinga and Sintra (good to a mile and a half) — soundings and the light will tell. I have put to the captain my offer to go ashore with the boat for the prices and news at Lisbon, as was offered and missed at Ferrol: the ore's market question — does Lisbon buy British copper ore, and at what — is the whole point of stopping here. Watching for brought up.

If the boat goes ashore at Lisbon for the prices and the news, I ask leave to be of it — I would bring off the port's list entire, the demand for our ore above all, and whatever news the quay holds of the wars and of what Lisbon wants. If the errand is Mr Bailey's alone once more, I shall ask him the questions when he comes off and set them in the ship's paper. As you please, sir.

The passenger, on the quarterdeck: The word on deck is the one I have been waiting for since Ferrol: the captain has agreed to Mr Jarvis's proposal — the turn is made east, she is steering SE for the Cascais road, and Lisbon herself is the errand. Four leagues off, the wind W and fair through the Belem road, and plain sail with hands ready to come to anchor below the light of Our Lady of the Guide.
